Andoni Iraola's Liverpool revolution continues, as another big-name transfer shapes up

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool and Bayern Munich might be about to shake hands on an intriguing transfer move in which big names move on either side.

The last two summers have been two of the biggest transfer windows in Liverpool's history, with three £100 million players joining the club in a recruitment revolution, following the end of the Jurgen Klopp era.

And things might be about to get even more extraordinary, with Bayern Munich “increasingly likely” to sell one of their biggest names – and the Reds front and centre for his signature.

Despite critics pointing to a lack of balance in their forward options over the summer, Liverpool are starting to find rhythm in attack under new manager Andoni Iraola, as the likes of Bradley Barcola, Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Rio Ngumoha all performed well in the weekend's 4-1 victory over Manchester United.

With Wirtz and Ngumoha both targets of Bayern Munich, however, the balance may be about to shift again – with the Bavarians now “increasingly likely” to sell Jamal Musiala.

Musiala has struggled this season with what he has described as “neurological dysfunction” this season, with honourary Bayern president Uli Hoeness has faced significant criticism for comments in which he questioned whether Musiala will ever return to his best form for Die Roten, stating, “What he is capable of delivering now is no longer what was stipulated in the contract” he signed at the Allianz Arena.

TEAMtalk reports that Liverpool and Arsenal are now interested in Musiala, with Bayern now potentially open to selling a previously untouchable asset – paving the way for either Wirtz or Ngumoha to leave.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

FourFourTwo understands that the latter is in talks over a new contract, but with Wirtz having struggled in English football since briefly becoming the Reds' all-time record transfer, he may welcome a return to the Bundesliga, where he made a name for himself as one of the biggest talents in world football and won the title with an invincible Bayer Leverkusen side.

It has recently been suggested in the German media that Wirtz and Musiala aren't naturally compatible in the same team, with journalist Christian Falk likening the pair's jostling for a place as Die Mannschaft's No.10 as similar to the battle between Gunter Netzer and Wolfgang Overath for a place in West Germany's 1974 World Cup side.

Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard, meanwhile, has been linked with a move to Bayern – while the Gunners could field Musiala on the left wing.

Transfermarkt values Musiala at €80m. Liverpool face Club Brugge tonight in Champions League action.

#882. A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains. Credit: 3DMedisphere/SPL

In the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV. Her story could have represented just another sobering statistic in the epidemic that was tearing through the region, but instead, she became a source of inspiration for scientists and of hope for millions. Enrolled in a study to track the course of newly acquired infections, the woman mounted a ferocious immune response to the virus over the next several years as doctors in the study treated her and took regular blood samples to monitor what was going on in her body.

Although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1. The woman is known in the literature as CAP256.

Scientists now think that by mimicking some of the key elements of an infection like hers, they might be able to train other people’s immune systems to make similarly potent antibodies that can block a diverse array of HIV strains. Ultimately, they say, they might achieve one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine that can stop HIV in its tracks.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

“We have a line of sight to an efficacious vaccine,” says Mark Feinberg, president and chief executive of the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) in New York City. “The scientific promise is greater than it’s ever been.”

This year, several teams described vaccination strategies that — in monkeys — can trigger the production of what are known as broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), molecules that can completely shut down an infection from a diverse range of HIV strains before it begins2–4. “No one has achieved that before. It’s a very important milestone,” says Rogier Sanders, a virologist at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

Humans who have received components of similar vaccines can produce precursors to these bnAbs5–7, suggesting that with further refinement, an effective vaccine is possible.

Success is by no means guaranteed, says Feinberg. HIV has proved a formidable foe for vaccine developers in the past. And there is another factor that adds complications. The availability of successful drugs, such as lenacapavir, that prevent HIV infection might make it difficult to test how well a vaccine works. Meanwhile, devastating cuts to the US funding that supported preclinical and clinical research for HIV have left some efforts on a precipice.

“We’re in a better position than we’ve ever been, and just at this time, we’ve seen the funding streams cut off,” says Dennis Burton, an immunologist and virologist at Scripps Research, a research institute in La Jolla, California.

The latest glimmers of success follow decades of failure. Initially, scientists looking to develop an HIV vaccine followed a strategy that had been successful for many other viruses, including hepatitis B: administer a lab-made version of the proteins that viruses use to attach to host cells and the body should start producing antibodies that will block infection. In HIV’s case, it’s the surface protein known as envelope that latches onto a molecular receptor on human T cells so that the virus can infect them. “There was only one protein, and so it seemed straightforward,” says Sallie Permar, a vaccinologist and paediatrician at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York City.

Starting in the 1980s, researchers made vaccines that contained the HIV envelope protein, to elicit antibodies against it, but the vaccines failed to prevent infection in clinical-trial participants. HIV mutates rapidly and most circulating strains were still able to mount an infection. “With HIV, there are millions of strains circulating simultaneously. Taking out one does nothing,” says Richard Wyatt, a viral immunologist at Scripps Research.

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Researchers tried other strategies, such as vaccines that recruited ‘killer’ T cells to wipe out infected cells, and those that delivered a wider diversity of proteins to overcome HIV’s penchant for mutation. In 2009, a clinical trial in Thailand reported modest signs of protection for a vaccine that triggered both T-cell and antibody responses8. But efforts to replicate those results failed, and that strategy was abandoned, too.

One overarching problem, says Feinberg, was that nobody knew what the immunological signature — the measurable biological response after injection — of an effective HIV vaccine looked like, so the only way to assess a candidate was to conduct large-scale efficacy trials and hope for the best. “It was all a shot in the dark,” says Burton.

That attitude began to change after the discovery of bnAbs. In the 1990s, teams led by Burton and microbiologist Hermann Katinger, then at the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences in Vienna, identified the first of them in individuals who were living with HIV9,10. These bnAbs could protect monkeys from infection by HIV strains circulating in Europe and America, but it took large doses, which were unlikely to be reached and sustained with a vaccine. And the protection was less effective against some strains from Africa.

In the 2000s, Burton’s team developed a way to sort through vast numbers of B cells — the immune cells that produce antibodies — for the rare ones that make bnAbs. After screening around 1,800 people living with HIV, they identified a pair of highly potent bnAbs, made by a donor in Africa, that blocked infection from dozens of HIV strains11. “That ignited the field,” says Burton.

Researchers would have to learn how to train the immune system to produce these kinds of bnAb. The strategies to do so emerged from the recognition that bnAbs often develop gradually in HIV-infected individuals such as CAP256. It happens through a sustained “cat and mouse game” between the fast-changing virus and an immune system struggling to keep up, says Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases and the University of Witwatersrand, both in Johannesburg, who analysed CAP256’s blood.

To mimic that struggle in an uninfected person, researchers first deliver a ‘priming’ immunogen — a portion or complete copy of HIV’s envelope. This shot awakens B cells, triggering them to divide and become active. Subsequent doses deliver distinct versions of the HIV envelope to first ‘shape’ and then ‘polish’ the antibodies produced. The goal is to guide the awakened B cells through a process called affinity maturation, in which the antibodies develop extensive mutations that improve their binding and breadth. The key is that the most capable B cells are recruited early and the antibodies that they produce are honed over time (see ‘Targeted vaccines’).

Source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

Sanders says that this strategy, sometimes known as germline targeting, is a bit like looking for an elite footballer among pools of youth players. Rather than trying to train everyone up to an expert level, they want to identify talent early and nurture it to superstardom. “We’re scouting the talented B cells,” Sanders says.

Researchers have taken different approaches to scouting these cells. After Moore and colleagues discovered CAP256’s antibodies, they sequenced the viruses circulating in her blood to identify what might have triggered and shaped the antibodies’ production.

A modified version of the envelope protein from one such virus has shown promise as a priming agent for the immune system in monkeys and is now being trialled in humans, says virologist George Shaw who co-led the preclinical work for this2 with virologist Beatrice Hahn, both at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

Another team, led by William Schief at Scripps Research, used computational structural modelling and cell studies to design immunogens that activate a specific subset of B cells that make antibodies capable of blocking the binding site through which HIV latches onto T cells5.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants

In small trials of vaccination with either protein or mRNA-based versions of this immunogen12, which is called eOD-GT8, nearly all participants developed ‘bnAb precursors’. These are antibodies with the desired genetic and structural characteristics of a bnAb that blocks the T-cell binding site on the envelope protein, but not the bevy of mutations that makes bnAbs elite. In participants who also got a booster shot of a different immunogen, the antibodies picked up mutations that improved their binding and neutralization abilities. “It worked beautifully,” says Schief, who is also vice-president for protein design at Moderna Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

#881. Jamal Musiala suffers hamstring injury amid difficult spell for Bayern Munich star

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The midfielder will be out of action ‘until further notice’, according to the Bundesliga club

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Jamal Musiala will be sidelined “until further notice” after suffering a muscle injury to his right hamstring, in another setback for the 23-year-old.

Musiala has struggled with repeated injury issues over the last two years as well as a neurological condition which has received enormous scrutiny in recent weeks.

He suffered a muscle tear in April 2025 and began suffering from absence seizures, which cause a brief and sudden lapse in awareness, the same month, two months after signing a contract extension with Bayern Munich.

The condition was not made public knowledge until this summer, with Musiala experiencing two of these seizures during pre-season games. Absence seizures can be managed with daily medication, and other elite athletes, including England rugby player Tommy Freeman, have been able to continue professional sporting careers while experiencing the condition.

Over the same period Musiala has endured repeated injuries: he broke his fibula during the Club World Cup in 2025 and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, then had a metal plate removed from his foot after this summer’s World Cup.

He has only recently returned from an absence induced by a hamstring tear, coming off the bench against Koln in the Bundesliga after two months out. He made an appearance as a second-half substitute in Bayern’s surprise 2-1 defeat to Lille in the Champions League this week, but has now suffered another setback.

Bayern Munich announced on Friday: “FC Bayern’s medical department diagnosed Jamal Musiala with a muscle injury in his right thigh today. Musiala will be out until further notice. Get well soon, Jamal!”

How Bayern have handled Musiala’s neurological condition has been heavily criticised after highly-publicised comments by several members of the club’s hierarchy.

Former board chairman Karl-Heinz Rummenigge cast doubt on the midfielder’s future, saying the “hefty sums of money” Musiala is paid are “not justifiable any longer”, and honorary president Uli Hoeness suggested his contract - which now runs until 2030 - should be reviewed if his illness and injury record prevents him returning to top form.

The comments sparked backlash, with players’ union Fifpro saying it was “deeply concerned” by the “pressure” placed on Musiala by such public remarks.

Stand-in captain Joshua Kimmich said after the Lille defeat: “What I don’t understand is the way this is being communicated in public. It must never happen that the burden is placed on a player. The club is obviously the top priority and bigger than a player, but it’s not bigger than a person. That’s an absolute no-go and it is not Bayern-like.”

Bayern have a raft of top players out with injuries including star striker Harry Kane, who tore ligaments in his ankle during the Koln game, as well as Michael Olise, Manuel Neuer, Luis Diaz and Serge Gnabry.

They sit second in the Bundesliga and 15th in the Champions League group phase table.

Aston Villa signed Alejandro Garnacho over the summer on loan - but the Argentine winger clearly isn't trusted by Unai Emery

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Aston Villa star Alejandro Garnacho is looking increasingly bereft in the Midlands following comments from manager Unai Emery.

After three wins in their opening three Champions League fixtures, Aston Villa have now lost their last two, with a 1-0 defeat to Galatasaray following the loss against Barcelona – and with Paris Saint-Germain and Borussia Dortmund on the horizon, the Europa League winners face an increasingly tough ask to finish within the league phase's top eight and avoid a play-off place.

It doesn't look hopeful for Garnacho to be involved in either match, following Emery's post-match comments in Istanbul.

TEAMtalk have described the Basque boss's 19-word statement on Garnacho's absence as “humiliating”, when asked about why the winger was excluded from the squad to face Gala.

Garnacho was once labelled as an exciting talent at Manchester United, but was shipped out to Chelsea at the start of last season in a move that would net the Red Devils pure profit on his sale, and failed to light up Stamford Bridge last season – before joining Villa on loan over the summer.

Despite this, the 22-year-old has played just seven times under Emery, all off the bench, with the Villa boss saying after the game, “Today the players who were here are who I think are the best players to be here with us.”

Garnacho will make his move permanent if he makes a certain number of appearances for the Villans this season, as he looks to replace Morgan Rogers, who left Villa Park for a club-record nine-figure fee over the summer.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

But rather like Liverpool's Harvey Elliott last term, the winger hasn't impressed Emery in his limited showings, having clocked up 96 forgettable minutes thus far in claret-and-blue.

Elliott played just four times in the Premier League under Emery after it became clear that the five-time Europa League-winning coach didn't see a place in his team for the England under-21 star.

Emery later described the loan move as “embarrassing for everyone involved”, publicly apologising to the player for a move that he believed stunted his development as a midfielder.

FourFourTwo understands that Villa are already looking to back out of a permanent transfer for Garnacho, who moved to Villa along with Nicolas Jackson from the Blues.

These deals are just two of a plethora between the two clubs in recent years, including Jadon Sancho, Axel Disasi, Ian Maatsen, Emiliano Martinez, Carney Chukwuemeka and Omari Kellyman, with both sides criticised for exploiting the Premier League's Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR).

Transfermarkt values Garnacho at €22m. Villa play Ipswich Town away this weekend, as Premier League action continues.

#879. Fury's manager says AJ called him to check fight was on

Spencer Brown has reaffirmed Tyson Fury's fight against Anthony Joshua will go ahead on December 11; Paris Fury retracted comments made in a new Netflix documentary that her husband had Schizophrenia; the British Boxing Board of Control cleared Fury to fight on Friday

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Tyson Fury's manager Spencer Brown revealed Anthony Joshua called him to check if their fight was still going ahead, after claims the 'Gypsy King' had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.

Paris Fury made the claims during a new Netflix documentary about her husband's life, but later retracted her comments, clarifying: "[Fury] doesn't have this condition and has never received a diagnosis."

While some had raised questions over whether the 38-year-old would be able to fight, the British Boxing Board of Control [BBBoC], on Friday, announced it had cleared Fury, adding he had passed pre-fight tests.

Speaking to Dev Sahni, Brown flatly dismissed claims that their December 11 fight was in jeopardy.

"Even Anthony Joshua rang me and said: 'Is this fight going on, because I've heard rumours that his licence…" Brown said.

"I said: 'One-million per cent [the fight is on], just turn up and be there. The fight's happening; it's unbelievable'."

Fury posted on Instagram on Friday night to explain how delighted he was about the launch of his new documentary TYSON FURY, urging fans to watch the film, before adding: "The journey continues, next stop December 11."

Netflix says it has worked to "update" the footage in light of Paris' clarification on Thursday.

The documentary explores Fury's experiences with depression, anxiety and bipolar disorder after they became acute following his 2015 world championship victory over Wladimir Klitschko.

Brown said the 38-year-old was more focused on his training rather than speculation about the fight.

"To him, it's a load of old rubbish from 10 years ago," Brown said.

"Obviously, it's reared its head. People have decided to make an issue of it, when there is no issue. And people panicked a little bit. So, there is no issue. The fight goes on."

Brown added: "It's been noted and everybody knows that Tyson has suffered from a mental illness. And we all know that. It's out everywhere.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"That was a long time ago, he's very happy, and I've never seen him in a better headspace, to be quite honest."

Fury's manager also revealed the lengths his team are going to to help the Wythenshawe-born fighter prepare for the bout.

"I speak to him nearly every day," he said.

"Some mundane things about, we have to make sure that he's travelled right and he's in his hotel and that wherever he's staying, every minute thing has to be done right, down to the windows being blacked out.

"Because he's on a different sleep pattern because they're fighting late at night.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"We have to make sure that he's got solitude, and he's happy, and he's smiling every day. His food is there, transport is there.

"His security are there. Everything has to be done to a specification."

Brown also issued a warning to Joshua ahead of the fight.

"If you're listening, Anthony Joshua, the fight's on," Brown said. "Get ready. Make sure that chin of yours is solid. Because it's going to need to be."

Roberto De Zerbi has hailed Luca Williams-Barnett’s new contract as a clear sign of Tottenham’s ambition.

Williams-Barnett marked his full debut for Spurs with a goal and assist in Saturday’s 2-0 win over Ipswich to justify the growing hype around the highly-rated 18-year-old.

It was followed by a new long-term contract for the teenager on Tuesday, which is understood to run until 2031, and ahead of Sunday’s trip to Sunderland De Zerbi stressed the importance of keeping hold of him.

“It’s great news for us, the extension of his contract, because if you see other big teams, big clubs, they are losing young talent in the same situations,” De Zerbi said.

“We have to say thanks to the club, because I think it was an important step for us, for the pitch, for the football, but also for the fans, because I think we gave a great signal with this extension of the contract.

“And if the agent of Luca, if the family of Luca, accept to stay and to extend the contract, it’s because they believe in the Tottenham project. So I think the credit is for the club.”

Williams-Barnett looks to be in line for another start at Sunderland due to the absence of several attacking players.

De Zerbi added: “You have to analyse many things.

“I think he is ready to play because he is a mature guy, he has the personality to play in every stadium, every game, but we have to analyse everything he has done this week.

“The debut in the first XI, the goal, the assist, the extension of his contract. Everything is for the best. For us, for him, for the club.”

De Zerbi used Dejan Kulusevski as an example for Williams-Barnett to follow and the Sweden playmaker could start one of Tottenham’s three matches over the next week after a 17-month absence with a serious knee injury.

“I am thinking to start maybe not now, but I think we are very close to start a game,” De Zerbi added.

“Deki is working well. I watched his games in the national team just to understand the physical condition.

“He played the first game as a winger and the second game as a number 10 and especially in the second game he played very well, but we have to be good to understand the right moment to put him on the pitch.

“I think medical staff, physical staff, they are working very well with him and we can’t lose any time, but we can’t take any risk because he is a special player.”

While Kulusevski is close to a start, Tottenham are set to be without Savio for the rest of 2026 and beyond due to a hamstring issue sustained late on against Ipswich.

De Zerbi said: “I don’t know, 50 days, 60 days, 80 days, I don’t know. When he comes back I think he will be crucial for us for the last step of the season.”

Newcastle United's owners PIF are seeking fresh investment to help the club achieve its infrastructure goals

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At first glance, headlines stating that Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) has put 25 per cent of Newcastle United up for sale were always going to draw intrigue and perhaps even alarm on Tyneside.

Five years on from the much-heralded takeover that ended Mike Ashley’s unpopular regime, any suggestion of the club’s sovereign wealth owners cashing in naturally invites fears that the project is running out of steam.

However, this proposed transaction is actually one of the more encouraging developments for Newcastle supporters in months.

First and foremost, PIF are not packing their bags and walking away from St James’ Park.

Rather than offloading existing shares to pocket a profit, the club is issuing brand-new equity - with US investment bank J.P. Morgan appointed to find an external partner.

This means not a single penny from the sale will flow back into PIF’s coffers - they are not recouping on their investment. Instead, funds raised through the share issue will supposedly be injected into Newcastle's ongoing projects.

PIF will see its majority stake diluted rather than exiting the club, remaining firmly in the driving seat as owners with majority control.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

While fans have grown increasingly frustrated by delays around major infrastructure upgrades, the club, led on the executive side by chief executive David Hopkinson, remains engaged in long-term plans to either substantially redevelop St James’ Park or build a brand-new stadium altogether, alongside the construction of a state-of-the-art training complex.

Bringing in additional investment allows Newcastle to raise hundreds of millions in fresh equity to accelerate those builds, sharing the heavy financial lifting.

After a difficult summer that saw stars like Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon depart to help balance the books, developing Newcastle’s infrastructure and off-pitch revenue streams is the only sustainable way to compete with Europe's elite.

Since original consortium member Amanda Staveley sold her shares and left the board in 2024, ownership of the Magpies has been split between just two parties: PIF holds an 84 per cent majority stake, while the London-based Reuben family - represented on the board by Jamie Reuben, via RB Sports & Media - owns the remaining 16 per cent.

Issuing new shares to cover a 25 per cent stake will dilute both PIF and potentially the Reubens proportionally, leaving PIF with comfortably over 60 per cent of the club and still overall control.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. Slegers led Arsenal to Champions League glory in May 2025

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Renee Slegers has left her role as head coach of Arsenal following a difficult start to the Women’s Super League season for the north London club.

The Gunners occupy sixth place in the WSL standings, sitting 12 points behind leaders Chelsea after 11 matches, and remain winless at home in the league this term.

The Dutch manager assumed the role from Jonas Eidevall, initially on an interim basis, two years ago before guiding Arsenal to Champions League glory in May 2025.

A statement on arsenal.com read: "We can confirm Renee Slegers has left her position as head coach of our women’s first team by mutual consent.

"Renee departs following a disappointing start to the 2026-27 season, with assistant coach Aaron D’Antino also leaving the club.

"The process of appointing a successor is under way and we will update in due course. Assistant coach Melissa Clarke-Reed will take charge of the team in the interim period.

"Everyone at Arsenal would like to thank Renee and Aaron for their contributions to the club and wish them every success in their future careers."

Pressure had been mounting on Slegers, particularly with Arsenal struggling to convert in front of goal, and her final match ended in a goalless draw against West Ham last Sunday.

Gunners director of women’s football Clare Wheatley said: "It was an extremely difficult decision to part ways with Renee, who has led the team with dedication and commitment throughout her time here.

"In leading us to glory in the Champions League and the inaugural Fifa Champions Cup, Renee has made a significant and lasting contribution to the history of Arsenal, with close support from Aaron.

"After careful reflection, it is clear that results have been below the expected level and change is necessary."

Arsenal have two weeks until their next fixture due to the international break, with England set to face Ukraine in a two-legged playoff as Sarina Wiegman’s side aim to secure their place at next year’s World Cup.

Once the international break finishes, Arsenal will return to action without Slegers when they travel to Everton on 11 December.

He apologised for the interview and boss Xabi Alonso said the matter was closed, but Friday’s Premier League game was a bad one for him.

The visiting supporters consistently jeered the centre-back when he was in possession in the first half. Fofana and his teammates endured a tough start at the City Ground as they fell behind to Igor Jesus’ brilliant fifth-minute strike.

A bad night got worse in the early stages of the second half when Fofana brought down Liam Delap for a penalty that Morgan Gibbs-White converted to double Forest’s lead.

Emmanuel Emegha did score to halve the deficit but Gibbs-White’s second goal restored Forest’s healthy advantage and although another late Emegha strike saw the Blues pile on the pressure to try and snatch an injury-time equaliser, they ultimately suffered a 3-2 loss that their poor performance deserved.

#871. Xabi Alonso under huge pressure as Chelsea slip to dispiriting defeat at Nottingham Forest

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Nottingham Forest 3-2 Chelsea: Morgan Gibbs-White scored twice to help condemn the Blues to a third straight loss and Alonso’s job suddenly looks precarious

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Chelsea slumped to a third successive Premier League defeat as they went down 3-2 at Nottingham Forest to mount the pressure on boss Xabi Alonso.

The London club were second-best to Forest, who won it through Igor Jesus’ brilliant opener and a Morgan Gibbs-White double after the break.

Emmanuel Emegha scored twice to give the scoreline a different complexion, but that does not mask the overall poor performance.

The latest loss comes after last weekend’s alarming 4-1 defeat to Leeds and Alonso has clear issues to address as they slide down the table.

One of them is Wesley Fofana after the Frenchman was booed and jeered by his own fans after an unauthorised YouTube interview where he appeared to joke about the club’s Carabao Cup exit.

Forest claimed back-to-back home wins after beating Manchester City last time out at the City Ground and this performance was an indication that they are moving in the right direction under Oliver Glasner.

Alonso opted to change his defence after last week’s debacle against Leeds, dropping Levi Colwill and replacing him in the back four with midfielder Moises Caicedo. The Spaniard did stick with under-fire Fofana, who was booed from the off.

Both men came under early pressure as Forest began well. Liam Delap, desperate to score against the club where his career stalled last season, had a snap-shot in the first minute, but Emiliano Martinez was not troubled.

But the Argentina goalkeeper could do nothing about a sublime Forest opener in the fifth minute. Daniel Munoz drilled in a cross from that right that Jesus sent into the top corner with an acrobatic volley. It was a fine piece of athleticism, even if contact did come off the shin.

That was the only real moment of quality in a first half where Forest were the better side. Alonso’s men had nothing going forward and failed to muster a shot on target.

Things did not improve after the break as Fofana’s night got worse. He lost out on a routine challenge to Delap, who burst clear into the box and was felled by the Frenchman.

Referee Andy Madley pointed to the spot and Gibbs-White stepped up and sent Martinez the wrong way.

But Chelsea got themselves back into it three minutes later, with their first shot on target, and they needed plenty of luck.

Pedro Neto’s shot hit Jair Cunha and it fell kindly into the path of half-time substitute Emegha, who rifled into the bottom corner.

Fofana was then hooked as he was put out of his mercy, but Chelsea still looked vulnerable.

James McAtee should have done better with his shot after a fine pass by Gibbs-White, while Murillo’s thumping volley from distance brought a good save by Martinez.

Forest restored their two-goal cushion in the 72nd minute as they scored an excellent third. Xaver Schlager picked up a loose ball, made space with a fine first touch and then found Gibbs-White with an incisive pass, which the England international coolly clipped home.

They appeared to be seeing the match out with ease, but that changed in the 89th minute as Chelsea scored out of nothing.

Neto’s cross found Emegha who headed home to set up a grandstand finish, but Forest held on for a deserved three points.

The more things change, the more they stay the same - Watford is an unmanageable club

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some things are certain in life; death, taxes and Watford sacking another head coach.

At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

It was the latest in a series of lifeless performances from a Watford side that have looked ill-equipped for Championship football from the moment the season started.

Now, at a time where Watford need Championship experience more than ever, owner Gino Pozzo has turned to former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu, a man that has had 13 jobs in 15 years, never managed more than 60 games at any team and most importantly, never played or coached in England or in one of Europe’s major leagues.

Given Watford’s reputation with head coaches, many would joke Iordanescu’s appointment sounds like a match made in heaven.

For Hornets fans, though, it’s an act of desperation from a club that has no plan, structure or hope.

In truth, Dionisi is the latest in a series of head coaches who have been let down by owner Pozzo, chairman Scott Duxbury and technical director Gianluca Nani, who seem incapable of building a squad or supporting a head coach.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Things could have been so different for the Italian, because at the start of the season, there was clearly something there. Watford were excellent in their opening day win over Southampton - playing with real flair and intensity in the first half - and followed that up with draws against Wrexham and West Ham. It was clear the players respected the Italian.

However, the warning signs were already there. In the summer, Dionisi and supporters were told that Watford would prioritise experienced players in the transfer market. None arrived.

Nestory Irankunda, Imran Louza and Giorgi Chakvetadze - three key players - were sold and not replaced, with Watford starting the season with just two centre-backs on the club’s books and two fit central midfielders.

The Italian sounded increasingly exasperated as his calls for reinforcements fell on deaf ears until the final few days of the window, where Watford eventually panicked and brought in Stephy Mavididi, Soumaila Coulibaly and Branimir Mlacic on loan. Myron Boadu and Michail Antonio arrived on free transfers.

Most of those players arrived unfit and come September, Dionisi was struggling to fill the bench as injuries took hold. The Italian never really recovered from embarrassing defeats to Burnley and Cardiff City, deploying a back five in recent weeks as he attempted to make the Golden Boys harder to beat.

Quite frankly, Watford are unmanageable. Not even Pep Guardiola would be successful at Vicarage Road, because no head coach is given the opportunity to implement a style of play when they have to contend with poor recruitment, a leadership vacuum and a dressing room with seemingly poor attitudes.

Rob Edwards was promised he'd be backed in the transfer market come hell or high water by chairman Duxbury in the summer of 2022. Most of the signings he received didn't fit his system and he was sacked within two months of the season starting.

After Edwards, Slaven Bilic thought he'd be able to sign players he wanted in the January transfer window. He received Joao Ferreira and Henrique Araujo - both of whom never looked suited to Championship football – as well as Ryan Porteous, Wesley Hoedt and Britt Assombalonga. Bilic was gone by March.

Then came Chris Wilder, who repeatedly called out the poor attitude within the dressing room and wasn't given a contract extension when his deal expired in the summer of 2023. After the wheels came off under Valerian Ismael, Tom Cleverley was promoted to head coach in 2024 and despite a thin squad, united the players and fans, having been a popular player at Vicarage Road during his playing days.

Once again, though, January arrived and Cleverley didn't get the options he so dearly needed, meaning Watford's form dropped off and he was sacked, somewhat harshly, at the end of the season.

Just last season, the popular Javi Gracia returned for a second spell in charge and had Watford in the play-off spots by January. He was promised additions, but none were forthcoming and ultimately the Spaniard decided the job wasn't worth his time. Gracia resigned, returning to Spain to spend time with his family.

In short, it's time the Watford ownership took a long, hard look at themselves, rather than the head coach. Has Iordanescu been appointed because no one sensible will take it? Any head coach worth his salt in England - and possibly now Italy, too - knows what they’re walking into.

In a recent interview with Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement, Pozzo tried shifting accountability for the club’s downfall, which can be traced back to the FA Cup Final in 2019. Since then, numerous decisions have, in the eyes of supporters, led to the erosion of the club's identity - fans have had enough.

Empty statements, the constant churn of players and head coaches, and what appears to be a lack of any real structure or plan - supporters are fed up.

The fact Watford closed their Under-21 setup, downgraded their academy and sold off the women's team this summer was a huge source of disappointment for fans, too, given the club’s rich history of bringing players through their youth system.

Unless there is a sudden change of approach overnight, Watford are only heading one way and that's down to League 1.

#869. How a green economy could help reverse climate change

Green growth promises a future in which economies thrive without destroying the environment. But is this vision realistic?

Human civilization is currently profoundly unsustainable. Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries critical for sustaining life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity.

If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.

It's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change. That's where the idea of green growth comes in.

Its promise is to keep growing the economy while reducing emissions and resource use. That involves, for instance, running factories, businesses and homes on wind, solar and other green energy instead of coal and gas, replacing gas-fired furnaces with heat pumps and  recycling and reusing resources and raw materials.

"Basically, the idea is: business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies," said Helmut Haberl, a social ecology professor at BOKU University in Vienna. Along with his colleagues, he published a major report in 2020 evaluating more than 800 studies on green growth.

In principle, the world's economic output could continue to grow in the long term and generate significantly fewer emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. That's been shown in scenarios modeled by researchers with the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC.

Thanks to renewable energy and green technologies, those scenarios have already become reality in several countries and regions.

The economies of developed countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Japanand Australia have experienced years of growth alongside sinking CO2 emissions. That's even when offshore production is included.

In the European Union, the bloc-wide economy has grown by more than 70% since 1990. Meanwhile, the EU's carbon emissions have dropped by around 40%.

But such a complete decoupling of growth and emissions is, according to Haberl and his fellow researchers, relatively rare.

In India, and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, economies are becoming more efficient. But while economic performance is outpacing emissions growth, emissions are still rising in those countries and globally. This is not compatible with preventing the worst impacts of climate change.

"That doesn't mean, however, that it couldn't work in the future," said Haberl, referring to decoupling of growth and emissions.

And even though economic growth has been shown to be compatible with emissions reduction, eliminating all greenhouse gases from a polluting industry like steel or chemicals is complicated.

These sectors don't just release emissions by burning fossil fuels for energy; carbon is also a key part of the chemical processes used to create their products, notably in the steel industry.

Replacing it with greener substitutes, or an alternative energy source like green hydrogen, requires significant investment.

There's another hurdle: the world's high consumption of resources. A productive economy depends on many raw materials and other products: ores, chemicals, wood, cement, glass and agricultural products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Many countries are now using green technologies to reduce the amount of resources needed to manufacture a product, for example, and are making their economies more efficient.

But that doesn't mean overall fewer resources are being used because falling costs can encourage businesses to produce more things and people to consume more. This can partially offset green savings and is called the rebound effect.

The British economy has been growing for years, emissions have been dropping and efficiency has increased, but the UK still used 7% more resources in 2023 than it did in 2001.

Global resource consumption has tripled over the last 50 years. If the world continues on the current pathway, that could increase by another 60% by 2060. It remains unclear whether green growth can deliver the emissions and resource reductions needed to stop climate change and biodiversity loss rapidly enough.

"We really need to move beyond efficiency gains in our existing production practices to look more broadly at what we consume," said Catherine Ganzleben, a sustainability and fair transitions expert at the European Environment Agency.

She told DW that people also need to reconsider how they consume and whether they really need to own everything they use in their daily life — cars, for example.

"But we can shift towards models where we share cars, so we pool our resources and have significantly lower resources per person through sharing the goods that we need."

Some researchers have concluded that unrestricted economic growth is no longer possible in the long term, even if it's sustainable.

Instead, they've called for degrowth. This posits slower economic growth, no growth at all or even negative growth, so that the world's ecosystems and the climate have a chance to recover and stabilize.

That applies mainly to economies in richer countries, which would need to take targeted steps to reduce their energy and resource use. Poorer countries would continue to grow until their economies and quality of life improve significantly.

Under the degrowth theory, a society's prosperity is not measured solely by the growth of its gross domestic product, but by values such as quality of life, education and community. The idea is that once countries develop to a certain point, additional growth doesn't translate into greater well-being.

Ultimately, the concept is based on the idea that human well-being and ecological sustainability is only possible in the long term with a planned, socially just reduction of material production and resource consumption. Degrowth advocates argue this would be preferable to an unplanned and potentially catastrophic economic contraction caused by escalating climate extremes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A 2020 study by researchers from the universities of Leeds and Lausanne showed that the concept of degrowth supported the world's climate goals — and that a high quality of life didn't have to be sacrificed in exchange for a significantly lower consumption of energy and resources.

However, there is still no conclusive evidence that an entire modern economy could continue to function entirely on the degrowth principles in the long term.

Nevertheless, Haberl doesn't assume that an environmentally friendly economic model automatically goes hand in hand with sacrifice, arguing instead for a needs-based economy.

"A society isn't necessarily better off when it's producing more goods and services," he said. It all depends on how prosperity and quality of life are measured in the future, and how states decide to do business.

Today, a successful economy is measured by the growth of a country's gross domestic product — put simply, the worth of all of its goods and services. This calculation doesn't account for income distribution, unpaid work, quality of life or environmental damage.

"The highest possible real incomes for every individual would probably not be compatible with ecological goals in the long term," said Haberl. "On the other hand, an increase in prosperity — related to a higher quality of life — would be."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An analysis by the European Environment Agency (EEA) pointed out that the idea of steady growth is part of the world's economic cycle, and deeply anchored in our institutions, norms and societal discourse. The job market and tax system are also closely tied to gross domestic product growth. A shrinking economy would therefore require a fundamental shift in our way of thinking.

Countries face a dilemma: a steadily growing economy is not compatible with ecological goals, according to the EEA. On the other side, a sharp decline in growth could trigger enormous social upheaval.

And the correlation is much more complex than the idea of "less is more," as highlighted by an EEA study in November 2021. "The fact that GDP growth has been harmful for the environment does not necessarily mean that declining GDP would be good for the environment," noted the report.

Achieving green growth while respecting environmental limits would require an "unprecedented decoupling of economic activity from environmental and climate pressures. Whether this is feasible is currently uncertain."

This article was originally written in German.

#867. Southampton beat Middlesbrough to claim Spygate bragging rights as Finn Azaz taunts former club

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Southampton were thrown out of last season’s play-offs over the Spygate scandal

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Goals from Ryan Manning and Finn Azaz earned Southampton a 2-0 win against Middlesbrough, securing the bragging rights in the first match between the clubs since last season's Spygate controversy.

Manning, making his 300th Championship appearance, broke the deadlock in the second half before former Boro forward Azaz punished a defensive error to double the lead. The result extended Saints’ unbeaten home run to 19 matches and moved them within four points of the league leaders.

The fixture carried significant context after Saints were removed from last term’s play-offs and hit with a four-point deduction this campaign for illegally observing training sessions carried out by Boro, Ipswich and Oxford.

Middlesbrough were restored to the play-offs as a consequence, though they ultimately missed out on Premier League promotion following a final defeat to Hull at Wembley.

While both managers sought to dismiss any lingering animosity beforehand, the contest carried clear competitive weight between two key promotion contenders.

Middlesbrough dominated the opening period, registering 11 attempts without finding a breakthrough. Leading scorer Will Lankshear squandered the best opportunities to add to his 15 league goals, firing straight at Daniel Peretz when put clean through in the 16th minute before directing a free header into the goalkeeper's midriff.

Callum Brittain also skimmed the crossbar with a cross, contributing to a frustrating run that saw Boro reach 49 away shots without scoring across their past three fixtures on the road.

Southampton had threatened earlier in the match, with Azaz striking the bar following a loose touch from Luke Ayling, while Radek Vitek produced impressive saves to deny Cyle Larin and Lewis Dobbin.

The home side eventually broke the deadlock after the break when James Bree lashed a low cross into the penalty area for Manning to divert into the net. The full-back celebrated by running directly to his manager.

Azaz, who moved to St Mary’s from Boro in the summer of 2025 following two seasons at the Riverside, sealed the victory in the 79th minute. Capitalising on a slip by Aidan Morris, the forward placed a cool finish into the bottom corner before running the length of the pitch to celebrate in front of his former fans while making a crying gesture.

The action sparked a late confrontation between the two sets of players, but Saints comfortably managed the remaining minutes to secure the points.

#862. The summer that changed Welsh football

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

You can listen to all three episodes of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football on BBC Sounds.

#861. Life as a Wag in the transfer window

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control."

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us."

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative."

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing."

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you."

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control."

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

#860. Are Manchester City living through their David Moyes era?
