#773. Lammens - the Man Utd goalkeeper under scrutiny like never before

Senne Lammens (left) joined Manchester United in the summer of 2025

After a first season at Manchester United that drew little but praise, goalkeeper Senne Lammens is under the microscope like never before.

A bad mistake that gifted Sporting their second goal on Wednesday, having earlier conceded a clumsy penalty, followed several other errors so far this season.

The 24-year-old Belgium international also made an error at the World Cup in the summer, spilling a shot that led to Spain's winning goal in the 88th minute of their quarter-final.

"I don't know [at what point Manchester United drop him]," legendary Manchester United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel told CBS Sports on Wednesday.

"Mauricio Pochettino has come in and brought his own staff. That means he's got a new goalkeeping coach and maybe that is something that can change it for him.

"[At the World Cup] he came on against Spain and made a bit of a mistake. Mikel Merino scored and they got knocked out. I feel he's lost a little bit of confidence from that mistake and hasn't really recovered.

"As a goalkeeper, when you're not on your best form, you need your defenders in front of you to help you out. The sad truth is that they haven't been able to do that and that makes it so much worse. I like him a lot but today was not a great day for him."

Director of football Jason Wilcox and United's data team overruled Ruben Amorim when they opted to sign Lammens from Royal Antwerp for Â£18.1m in September 2025.

Amorim wanted Argentina World Cup winner Emiliano Martinez, who was left waiting for a deadline day call that never came to seal a move from Aston Villa.

United felt Lammens had the attributes to become one of the world's best goalkeepers. At 24, he is still young. Schmeichel was 27 when he joined United in 1991. Edwin van der Sar was 34 when he left Fulham in 2005. Both had hundreds of senior appearances behind them. Lammens has just over 100, more than half of them with Royal Antwerp.

Although he made the odd error last season, Lammens did nothing to suggest Wilcox and co had got it wrong.

After releasing Turkey international Altay Bayindir, who replaced Andre Onana as first choice at the start of last season and is back on loan in Turkey with Trabzonspor, they signed 36-year-old Wales international Karl Darlow as back-up this term.

Darlow finished last season as first choice at Leeds. But he only started 30 league games in three seasons with the Elland Road outfit. Also on the bench in Lisbon was Tom Heaton. The 40-year-old has not played in a senior game since February 2023.

Mistakes earlier in the season â former United midfielder Paul Scholes claimed in September '"the jury is still out" on whether Lammens is truly top class â have brought increased analysis. His positioning for Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal for Liverpool on Sunday was questioned externally, even if United focused their attentions on Bradley Barcola shoving into the wall.

Just 75 seconds after getting down to make an excellent save from Luis Suarez's first penalty, Lammens recklessly charged out and upended Maxi Araujo, even though Noussair Mazraoui seemed to be in a position to deal with it.

Then, after two Bruno Fernandes goals at the start of the second period had turned the Champions League tie in the visitors' favour, Lammens reached to collect a high ball and inexplicably dropped it in front of Suarez, who applied the overhead kick finish.

Understandably, there was sympathy in the dressing room.

"This team is a family," said striker Joshua Zirkzee. "There's no-one who will suffer by themselves.

"Senne is a great goalkeeper and mistakes happen. In this moment, we just give him space. I'm not sure if he wants to hear anything at all. But Senne's a great kid. He's got a good head on him. We didn't draw because of him, and we all know that next game he is going to be at the top of his game."

'One mistake from being dropped' - Ashley Young on Senne Lammens

Toni Jimenez is Pochettino's long-time goalkeeping coach.

His arrival triggered the exit of Craig Mawson, who had been with Manchester United since 2019. Connor King is Jimenez's assistant but a relative newcomer himself, having joined from Burnley in 2026.

By its nature, goalkeeping at the highest level can be a mental challenge as well as a technical one. As Onana discovered, flaws can quickly become major issues and once the spotlight is shining, the attention is fierce.

Lammens has given the impression privately of being strong. He has seemed remarkably unaffected by his World Cup torment â his mistake against Spain came after he was introduced as a 71st-minute replacement for injured veteran Thibaut Courtois with the quarter-final delicately poised at 1-1. But only he knows the full picture.

Jimenez will be Pochettino's guide over what to do about the situation, although for now, Lammens' head coach is behind him.

"This type of thing happens," he said. "That is football. Football is about making mistakes.

"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.

"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better."

Following Wednesday's draw in Lisbon, Pochettino highlighted "two things" that need to improve if United are to start winning matches on a regular basis.

The first of those is the club's preferred goalkeeper. Of the 17 Premier League goalkeepers to have played a minimum of 10 matches in all competitions in this campaign, Lammens has the second-worst save success rate, keeping out just 60.2% of the shots he has faced. Only Coventry's Carl Rushworth (54.4%) has fared worse so far this season.

Lammens also ranks bottom of those 17 goalkeepers for clean sheet ratio (6.3%).

And there is substance to the suggestion that Lammens has declined in 2026-27. He made just one error leading to a goal in the entirety of last season in contrast to two already in this campaign. The data also shows that he is currently preventing far fewer goals.

The second "thing", however, has significant bearing on the first.

Clean sheets and conceding fewer goals are clearly a collective responsibility, particularly for the "defensive line" that Pochettino referenced on Wednesday - and United's defence has collectively struggled this season.

They have now let in 36 goals in all competitions, the most of any team in Europe's top five leagues. They have also conceded five penalties and received five red cards - both the second-highest tallies among Europe's elite divisions.

So is Lammens more error-prone this season? Apparently yes. But he's also playing behind a defence that, on current form, may not inspire too much confidence in their goalkeeper.

#772. The local boy aiming to be at the heart of Cardiff's derby aims

Colwill has one goal and three assists from 10 Championship appearances following Cardiff City's return to the Championship

Rubin Colwill is used to being in the centre of things.

He has been the focus of an ongoing argument over his role - or lack of it - in Craig Bellamy's Wales side.

It has meant the midfielder has been the subject of countless questions around international weeks, the latest prompting the Wales boss to ask a journalist if he had a Colwill poster in the middle of his bedroom wall.

The debate has stemmed from the 24-year-old being at the heart of Brian Barry-Murphy's stylish transformation of Cardiff City.

So it is understandable that, as he prepares to lead his boyhood club into the eye of the storm that is the south Wales derby, he is again in the centre of things.

And fitting for someone who grew up in the middle of the rivalry between the two cities.

"I took a lot of stick," Colwill said. Well, we presume that is what he might have said, stopping himself from swearing to describe life as a Cardiff fan from the town of Neath, nine miles from Swansea.

"I probably felt it more than most being surrounded by Swansea fans and a lot of mates being Swansea fans.

"It was tough because they were in the Premier League for a long spell, so I was always trying to give a bit back when we won a game or did well."

Bellamy an influence as Williams leads Swansea

Bellamy jokes reporter has Colwill poster in bedroom

Latest Cardiff City news, analysis and fan views

Colwill was always Cardiff, as was brother Joel, his team-mate for club and country.

Their mother - from Port Talbot, a little further east with a denser amount of support that turn towards the capital - was a Cardiff fan and so were her boys, signing for the club while still in primary school.

He has never gone to a derby in Swansea as a fan - he was never allowed - but was part of the Cardiff side that last won at their rivals in 2021 and has told team-mates all about the journey down the M4, where fans flock to bridges and encouragement turns to abuse as the miles clock up.

He will mention that, and the feeling of the times where, by his own admission, Cardiff were not good enough in a string of defeats that sting more than most.

But he will also share the "no better" feeling of being in the middle of the celebrations of a derby win, as he was in January 2025.

Colwill: 'Tough' growing up as a Cardiff fan

That Cardiff 3-0 victory was a rare high point in a season that eventually saw the club relegated from the Championship and in desperate need of a rebuild.

They have done just that, transitioning into an eye-catching, exciting team, who - depsite failing to win away this season and going into the game on the back of a 4-0 defeat by Preston North End - are ready to show Swansea the Bluebirds are a different beast these days.

Colwill and his influence has been very much a central cog in that change.

He has been game time and responsibility by Barry-Murphy - including the armband that might not be obvious for such a seemingly laidback character.

The academy product says he has learned much from the journey, including a frustrating spell of injuries that have limited his impact to seven starts since the return to the Championship.

It has seemingly been noticed by Bellamy, who spoke before Wales' recent Nations League defeat to Portugal about how he has improved as a player.

"There has been a big change in his game," Bellamy said, a former academy coach of the talented midfielder.

"He is a player I really like watching - before I did and I didn't. Now I see a lot of good things."

Colwill responded with a man-of-the-match performance against Portugal in what was his first competitive Wales start in five years.

"It was almost like I got to experience my first game twice," smiled Colwill.

Bellamy - who has questioned Colwill's work off the ball - has said he felt able to be more "ruthless" with the youngster because of their long association.

"Everyone knows," said Bellamy of what he thought Colwill needed to do to improve. "And none more than him."

Williams to lead Swansea in south Wales derby

Frozen out Robinson told he has Cardiff future

Despite being in the middle of it all, Colwill has not changed in playing personality, and certainly showed no pressure when he reclaimed his Wales spot.

Clearly there is a resilience that goes beyond sticking with a Cardiff scarf in an area full of Swansea colours.

"I've tried to learn from those experiences and develop myself mentally and improve my resilience so I can almost take anything that comes my way," he says.

"I think that's a massive part of football: you've got to stay grounded, stay focused, regardless if you're doing really well or really badly because it's a massive part of the game to stay consistent in the end."

So what of the challenge to improve and being in the middle of the two different approaches to getting the most out of him?

"I think they're very similar," is Colwill's response. "They both want to control the game, the structure, the body shape, how they want us to play, the press and reaction to giving the ball away.

"In the fundamentals of the game, they're similar. Obviously they're both different people so the approaches to that are very different, and it's in the little details.

"With Craig, he's always had that approach of if he thinks you can offer something or improve on, it's on us to take it on board and be open to that constructive criticism.

"It's not always easy. I think he does have a high demand of you, but if you do make a change as he asks of you then he will play you."

Cardiff players will have 'edge' against Swansea

After the stick, the carrot at Cardiff is the chance to follow in Bellamy's footsteps by scoring a winner in the derby at Swansea, as the Wales boss did in 2011 - Cardiff's last win there in front of travelling supporters.

Colwill smiles at the thought, just as he winces at the memories of the defeats - as a player and a fan - which is why he will not be telling team-mates to treat this game like just another.

"That attitude is almost like trying to protect yourself from the pressure," he argues. "But it's not. We have a lot of boys from the area who have come from the academy who really get the game and understand the whole picture of it and how important it is for everyone in the city.

"And we've got no fear of failure - if we lose we just leave it all out there, but we have full belief we can win."

If they do, it will come as no surprise if Colwill is at the heart of it.

#771. What went wrong for Alonso's Chelsea at Forest?

Sky Sports analyses the decisions from Xabi Alonso that contributed to Chelsea's 3-2 defeat to Nottingham Forest; Wesley Fofana started despite his controversial interview, while Levi Colwill was dropped; Xabi Alonso called for fundamentals but Chelsea were outrun

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Xabi Alonso called for his Chelsea side to get back to the fundamentals before kick-off - and then watched on as they were outworked and outclassed on their way to a miserable 3-2 defeat at Nottingham Forest.

"Everyone in the club and team, we need to stick together and go through this moment. We have to deal with it and we are responsible," Alonso told Sky Sports after the game, which marked their third successive defeat in the Premier League.

"It is a difficult moment for everyone at the club. For the team and the fans. Disappointed to lose again but we need to keep trying to find solutions.

"We can't stop. We are low in confidence. At this level you need to hold results and not concede so much. That is why we are losing."

Alonso now has as many losses in 15 games across all competitions as he did in 34 for Real Madrid (6). Since March, no side has more defeats in the top-flight than the Blues (14). And their problems are mounting by the day.

Here, Sky Sports analyses the decisions that contributed to the worrying defeat at the City Ground.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Despite the calls from Alonso to strip the game back to basics and get the fundamentals right, Chelsea felt short from minute one.

At the half-time interval, facing a 1-0 deficit and with zero shots on target, Chelsea had ran 3.8km less than Oliver Glasner's side.

The Forest boss was then quick to point out that they had outrun their opponents by 6km after the game. Yes, Chelsea had more possession, but they were also well behind in high-speed runs.

"I've seen one team jogging after the ball and one team sprinting after the ball and in this day and age, you cannot do that," said Jamie Redknapp.

"Distance covered is not always the barometer, but one thing is for sure, high-speed runs will tell you everything."

Starting Wesley Fofana in the same week the player had to apologise for his controversial interview, where he said he can "laugh about" the penalty miss that contributed to their Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool and contemplated retirement during injury spells at the club, was a bold move from Alonso. It did not pay off.

The tone was set early on. Fofana's first touches were heavily booed by the travelling Chelsea fans who had made the 130-mile journey in the cold and rain to watch their side slip to yet another dismal defeat.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The centre-back could only watch on as Igor Jesus volleyed in his stunning opener but was at the centre of attention, for all the wrong reasons, for the second.

After misjudging the ball while battling with former teammate Liam Delap, who caused problems all evening, Fofana rushed to atone for his error and fouled the striker in the penalty area.

Morgan Gibbs-White doubled the lead from the spot and ultimately the comeback, led by substitute Emmanuel Emegha, fell short.

He was cautioned for the challenge and eventually taken off for Levi Colwill, who was dropped by Alonso instead of Fofana, and the fans booed him once again.

"It didn't feel like a game for him tonight. He had a bad week with the podcast," said Jamie Redknapp after the game.

"By playing Fofana tonight, you created that. It was inevitable. He is lacking so much confidence; he needs some time.

"He is having a real difficult run of it at the moment."

After making the decision to drop Colwill, options at the centre of defence were limited with Maxence Lacroix and Reece James both sidelined.

Playing Josh Acheampong at centre-back and giving a rare start to Malo Gusto, an unused substitute on the night, seemed the more obvious choice but Alonso opted to play Moises Caicedo, arguably the best midfielder in the league, in the back four instead.

He was then tasked with dealing with a strike partnership of Delap and Igor Jesus. A difficult task for even the tallest of centre-backs, let alone a makeshift one standing at 5-foot-10.

He gave space to the Brazil striker for the opener and his presence in midfield was missed. He still led the way with 114 passes on the night, but Chelsea needed him in the middle of the park to deal with the likes of James McAtee and Xaver Schlager.

"They have bought players but if they do not sign a centre back, they cannot compete," said Redknapp after the game. He is right.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Alonso admitted that Emegha's performance after scoring twice off the bench was the lone positive for his side to take from their trip to the East Midlands. "For sure, he is having a good impact," he said. "He has done well. That is a positive."

He scored his first goal in the 4-1 defeat to Leeds United last time out but lost his place in the starting line-up on Friday.

Danny Welbeck, 36, was given the nod ahead of him and his performance mirrored the struggles Chelsea had as a unit.

Alonso called on the experience of Jordan Henderson and Welbeck to help weather their current struggles but it only whipped up the storm.

Welbeck was a bystander in the first half and had just seven touches before being replaced at the break, Emegha then scored with his first two to help spark hopes of a comeback.

His header for the second, holding off Jair Cunha, was one of the rare moments Chelsea matched the physicality of their opponents. He has to start moving forward without Joao Pedro available.

Alonso said the only way he knows how to address these issues is to attack them on the training ground. He has just five days to do that before they are put to the test against Crystal Palace, live on Sky Sports, who will be desperate for a win.

#770. Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?

From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.

The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."

France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

#769. DWTS Cohost Julianne Hough Addresses Criticism of Season 35 Fashion

Dancing With the Stars cohost Julianne Hough reacted to fans criticizing her style choices on season 35: “When you get into your late 30s, you just don’t give a f--k anymore.”

Julianne Hough is spinning away from the negativity.

After the Dancing With the Stars cohost made waves for her fashion choices during season 35, she shed insight into her looks while responding to those who gave a low score on her style.

“I really feel like I’m at this next inflection of my career,” Hough told Glamour in an interview published Nov. 24 alongside her stylist Brad Goreski. “When you get into your late 30s, you just don’t give a f--k anymore. You’re like, ‘Who am I? What do I want to wear? What makes me feel incredible?’ It has more intention rather than trying to fit into what’s hot.”

“I feel like I’m in my leading lady era,” she continued. “I mean that in the actual projects that I’m doing, but also me as a person.”

To cohost this season of DWTS alongside Alfonso Ribeiro, the professional dancer decided to take a step out of her usual style comfort zone.

“I’ve gone a little bit more vixen-y this year than I have girl next door because we’re trying to find that character,” she shared. “It’s been very strategic.”

As she twirled with a new vibe, Hough took some fashion risks, including a sultry Valentino ensemble—which featured a skin-colored bodysuit under a see-through skirt—during the Nov. 17 episode that really had fans talking, with one social media user calling for Hough’s stylist to be “fired” in a viral Instagram video.

But as for Goreski, he doesn’t believe the online chatter about Hough’s looks is completely pointe-less anyway, emphasizing that “any conversation, good or bad, around fashion is great.”

“I think Jules ultimately brings the looks to life,” he added, praising his client. “I’m glad that there’s another part of the show that people talk about. Not every person’s going to love every look. I know that from being a stylist for 15 years. And that’s okay.”

And ultimately, Hough concluded that taking those fashion risks is worth it, despite what people may say.

“Apathy is the enemy,” she said, sharing the phrase became her motto for the season. “The reason things exist and have charge and stay visible [is] people either love it or hate it. They still want to talk about it.”

As Hough and DWTS wrap up another season, read on for a deep dive into the reality TV series…

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

#768. Bournemouth 'allowed to dream' as fans book Europa League final hotels

Marco Rose replaced Andoni Iraola - who ended up at Liverpool - in the summer

Bournemouth are dreaming of winning the Europa League after staging a 10-man fightback to join a select band of teams to win their first five European games.

The Cherries trailed 1-0 to Iago Aspas' goal at Celta Vigo, and then went down to 10 men midway through the first half when Bafode Diakite was sent off.

But second-half goals from Alvaro Rodriguez and Rayan gave the Cherries a 10th consecutive win in all competitions, extending their club record run.

Bournemouth are only the third side to win each of their first five European matches (excluding qualifiers and including the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup), after Nuremberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73.

They top this season's table as the only club to win five out of five - and are closing in on a top-eight spot, which would mean they skip a play-off round and go straight into the last 16.

Some fans have told the BBC they have already booked hotels in Frankfurt for the final on 26 May.

As supporters sang about reaching that game, midfielder Alex Scott was asked for his thoughts on TNT Sports.

"Of course that's our dream. When you grow up wanting to be a footballer you dream of winning trophies," Scott said.

"Where this club has come from to where it is now, full credit to everyone who has built it.

"For players, it's a dream to be on the pitch playing for this club. We have still got wins to get to qualify into the top eight, and from there all focus is on pushing forward and hopefully we can go on and win it."

'Living the dream' - Bournemouth fan after Europa League win

The Cherries are in unprecedented times, with their biggest trophy to date being when they won the second-tier Championship in 2014-15.

In terms of cups, they won the 1983â84 Associate Members' Cup - which later became the EFL Trophy.

Head coach Marco Rose, who replaced Andoni Iraola in the summer, said: "It's always allowed to dream.

"If you get a competition like this you want to achieve the best possible thing. We know it's far away to go. Many games. Now it's about getting into the top eight to avoid more games and then we can see step by step."

As well as just winning their games, Bournemouth are firing in the goals. They have netted at least twice in each match during this 10-game winning run.

And they are the first side to score at least twice in each of their first five matches in Europe since Queens Park Rangers in 1976.

The win on Thursday was made even more impressive by the fact they contested 75% of the game with 10 men.

It came days after Manchester United seemed to implode after an early red card against Liverpool, losing 4-0.

Former England manager Glenn Hoddle said on TNT: "They have deserved this result. They've played beautifully with 10 men - probably as good as I've seen a team play defensively and with the ball.

"I've not seen a team go down to 10 men for so long and dictate a game and deserve to win the game. They were absolutely brilliant."

Cherries boss Rose told BBC Radio Solent: "What a team, what a spirit, what an energy.

"I said to Ty [Tyler Adams] sometimes it's not about tactics and formations and stuff like this. [David] Brooks did a great job when we got one player less - he played right defender like he played it for 10 years. We changed in the right moment. Everyone did his job on a really high level.

"We were just relentless and we never stopped to believe in this win and that's why big, big, big congratulations to the team.

"You feel if you're one player down that it's a difficult night, but to handle a difficult night like this, it just shows the character of the team and of the whole group."

The coach's belief in what they are doing filters through to the players.

Amine Adli, who set up the equaliser, told the BBC: "At half-time, everyone still believed we can turn the game in our way and this is what happened.

"Everyone was like 'guys we can make it, we have to believe. If we score the game can change.'"

Earlier this month, the attacking midfielder said he saw a lot of similarities to the Bayer Leverkusen team he was part of in 2023-24.

That is not a bad comparison, considering they went unbeaten to win the domestic double, as well as reaching the Europa League final.

So who can blame the Cherries for dreaming?

#765. McInnes tempers 'anxiety' as Rangers seek top spot

Ryan Naderi has netted some crucial goals for Derek McInnes this term

Derek McInnes says Rangers should not experience any anxiety about the prospect of going top of the Scottish Premiership as the Ibrox side look to extend their four-match winning run.

Rangers host in-form Falkirk on Saturday (15:00 GMT), who have won six on the bounce in the league, and victory would move McInnes' team top before leaders Celtic travel to face Hearts on Sunday.

"I don't think there should be anxiety when you're trying to go top of the league at all," McInnes said.

"Obviously, you want to be top of the league come the end of the season.

"If you've got an opportunity to go there, it's important you try and take it."

Ryan Naderi netted an early second-half equaliser then set up Djeidi Gassama as Rangers turned a 1-0 deficit into a 3-1 lead before Aberdeen scored a consolation in Tuesday's Premiership match at Ibrox.

It was Naderi's 11th goal of the season and McInnes spoke of his awareness of the now Czech Republic international last season while managing Hearts, who have used a data analytics firm for much of their recent recruitment.

"Last January, obviously, when we first saw that Rangers were linked with Naderi, like everything else, I would say to [Hearts sporting director] Graeme Jones, 'how do they rate him?'

"Because you're always curious, it's just the way it is. It's brilliant when you see other teams round about you signing a player that's not rated!

"He was someone that I think was well known to them. Brugge had an interest in Ryan, I think, and I think USG potentially had an interest in him as well but the kind of money, the fee, it just went away from them.

"The feeling was that he could help Rangers and make them better.

"I had a good conversation with Ryan when I first came in the door and what we felt this season could look like for him.

"He's stood up brilliantly to the injuries to Youssef [Chermiti] and Lawrence [Shankland] and he's had to be the guy. He's led the line brilliantly and I love the goals he scores. All top strikers have intelligence to be in the right place at the right time."

Rangers 'dug it out' despite naivety & complacency - McInnes

Visit our Rangers page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

And the manager reiterated his stance about keeping hold of assets like Naderi through January.

"These conversations that I have with Jim [Gillespie, chief executive] on a regular basis about players that we should be speaking to and trying to address and secure and give them a wee bit more security and a wee bit more comfort for us, these conversations, I think, have been ongoing," McInnes said.

"The club's well aware of what needs to be done and what we shouldn't be doing and Ryan's been part of that conversation."

McInnes' side won 2-1 away to Falkirk in September but the Bairns held Danny Rohl's Rangers to a 0-0 draw at Ibrox last season.

"What they have got is a bit more physicality," McInnes said of the Bairns.

"They can play when they want to play so they've mixed it up a bit this season, I think, and been a wee bit more pragmatic maybe at times as well, but they've still had those results that's got them where they are in the league and we've got a difficult game ahead of ourselves."

#764. Lyon dropped by Australia for Test series vs New Zealand

Nathan Lyon left out of Australia's 13-player squad for Test series at home to New Zealand, which starts in Perth on December 9; uncapped off-spinner Corey Rocchiccioli and batter Jack Clayton called up; Tests will also take place in Adelaide, Melbourne and Sydney

Nathan Lyon has been dropped by Australia for their four-Test series at home to New Zealand, with the veteran replaced by fellow off-spinner Corey Rocchiccioli.

Lyon, a mainstay for the Baggy Greens for 13 years, has not spoken publicly since Usman Khawaja's explosive Sandpapergate claims were published in his autobiography.

Australia selection chair George Bailey confirmed that the 39-year-old's omission for a series that starts in Perth on December 9 was not related to the ongoing saga but based on performances.

Pat Cummins (captain), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Jack Clayton, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Michael Neser, Matt Renshaw, Corey Rocchiccioli, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc.

Tom Latham (captain), Tom ​Blundell, Devon Conway, Jacob ​Duffy, Matt Fisher, Dean Foxcroft, ⁠Matt Henry, Kyle Jamieson, Daryl Mitchell, Henry Nicholls, ⁠Will O'Rourke, Glenn Phillips, ​Michael Rae, Rachin Ravindra, Nathan ​Smith, Will Young.

The uncapped Rocchiccioli, who has taken 205 wickets in 59 first-class matches and last week scored his maiden century, could debut on his home ground at Optus Stadium in the series opener.

Other notable omissions include Marnus Labuschagne, Cooper Connolly and Beau Webster, with middle-order batter Jack Clayton drafted into the squad and in line for a first appearance.

Bailey said to reporters of Lyon: "Nathan has not quite had the impact we would like with the ball in recent matches.

"[It was a] challenging conversation and the key to that conversation from the panel's point of view was we hope it's not the end for him."

Australia head to India for a five-Test tour following the series against New Zealand and Bailey indicated Lyon would be a likely inclusion for that trip if he wanted to extend his Australia career.

Bailey added: "I think he can still have enormous value when you project forward to India.

"Given his record there, his experience and his knowledge, and how challenging a place that is to tour, and the fact we've got five Tests there, no, I don't think [he would miss out].

"But understandably, it was a tough conversation for him. I think he's taking a little bit of time."

In recent years, Lyon has seen his role with the Test side diminished, with a right hamstring injury, sustained during day five of the third Ashes Test in 2025, ruling him out of Test selection for eight months.

Lyon, who ranks second as Australia's all-time leading wicket-taker behind Shane Warne with 577 wickets from 145 Tests, had previously been dropped for the second Ashes Test at The Gabba.

He spoke openly about the omission, saying he was "filthy" and "gutted" about being dropped.

Lyon had also been omitted from Australia's second Test against South Africa in October.

Prior to last year's Test at The Gabba, the off-spinner had remarkably not been left out of a Test squad since he made his debut in 2011.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rocchiccioli will likely go head-to-head with seamer Scott Boland for a spot in the side to play New Zealand on the fiery Perth pitch in the first Test.

"Corey has been a strong performer in domestic cricket for the past few seasons and has traits that are well suited to Australian conditions," Bailey said.

Under-scrutiny skipper Pat Cummins will captain the side, while Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Steve Smith, who have all found themselves at the centre of Australia's recent Sandpapergate saga, were also named in the group.

Smith had missed Australia's final Test against South Africa in Cape Town with a neck injury.

Australia will add one final player after the sixth round of Sheffield Shield matches.

First Test (December 9-13): Optus Stadium Perth

Second Test (December 17-21): Adelaide Oval

Third Test (December 26-30): MCG, Melbourne

#763. Iordanescu ready for Watford 'challenge'

Edward Iordandescu is the first Romanian to manage in the top four tiers of English football

New Watford boss Edward Iordanescu says he has inherited a "challenge" but also "an opportunity" as the club seeks to pull away from the Championship relegation zone.

The 48-year-old has replaced Alessio Dionisi, who was sacked on Sunday after only five months in charge, following a run of seven defeats in 10 league games.

Iordanescu became Watford's sixth new boss in less than 18 months and is the 25th manager since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

He will take charge of the Hornets for the first time on Saturday when they travel to bottom club Derby County.

The Romanian met the media for the first time on Friday, and set out his vision for his tenure.

The Watford job is Iordanescu's first since leaving Legia Warsaw in October 2025, having won the Polish Super Cup with them last season.

It is the 10th managerial post of his 15-year coaching career, which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj - who he guided to the Romanian title and two domestic cups after joining midway through the 2020-21 season.

He also spent two and a half years in charge of Romania, guiding them to the last 16 of Euro 2024, where they were beaten by the Netherlands.

However, in his first job in English football, he inherits a Watford side three points above the drop zone and facing a fight for their second-tier status.

"I'm proud more than anything else and I'm honoured and happy to be here, but I'm also very aware of the challenge in front of me," Iordanescu told BBC Three Counties Radio.

"I don't want to make promises. I know the fans are not happy in this moment, but also I know that my words are not enough to bring them back, so they wait for facts. We need that, but of course there is a lot of work to do, there is a process in front of us and I hope we make the next steps right away.

"For me it's a challenge but at the same time it's an opportunity and I want to transform this opportunity into something good for the club, for the fans. This is the most important [thing]."

Prior to the dismissal of Dionisi, former Watford player Tom Ince - who left the club at the end of the 2025-26 season - told the BBC's 72+ Podcast there was "so much control away from the manager" at Vicarage Road.

While Ince, now at League Two side Tranmere Rovers, added his respect of positives of chairman Gino Pozzo's practises, he is not alone in speaking out about the board's influence.

Former England boss Sam Allardyce stated he turned down the Watford job in 2019 after claiming he was told how the side should play and which players should be in the XI.

But Iordandescu revealed that is not his expectation.

"I know my borders and I know my responsibilities." he said. "I'm in this club with a lot of quality people, professionals, people that know, understand, in detail, football, but starting yesterday I'm the number one in the technical side.

"I don't believe there's somebody here in the club that can overcome the coach, taking the technical knowledge, so it will be my responsibility, but also the technical part will be my decision all the time."

Pioneer or coach-eater? The complex world of Pozzo's Watford

From a purely statistical perspective, Watford's laboured start to the season under Dionisi could be credited to one key deficiency.

The Hornets have scored the fewest goals in the Championship, with only 13 in their 17 matches so far.

However, Iordanescu said his primary objective was not to thrill, but to win.

He said: "I always prefer to win 1-0 than 4-2. One-nil means you have an organised team, a team with some responsibility to engage 100% and to give everything for the result.

"So for me the priority is not to score more goals - [it is] to start to be organised, to start to act and react together on the pitch, to start to understand that the mindset should be a little bit different than what it was until now and to start to be efficient.

"In time we will see about scoring more goals, definitely every coach wants the team to score as much as possible."

Iordanescu also appeared to confirm he was in talks about taking over while Dionisi was still in charge.

It was reported on 12 November that the Hertfordshire club were in talks with him, but Dionisi, who had only been appointed in June, remained in charge across the international break and for Saturday's 4-0 defeat at Sheffield United.

The Italian was sacked on Sunday, with Iordanescu appointed on Wednesday.

Iordanescu said he had "asked for time" from the Watford hierachy before accepting the role.

He said: "I wanted to understand very clearly the objectives, the targets, so when I gave the final response, I was aware of everything.

"I'm here, I'm enthusiastic, I'm positive, I'm confident we can do good things together, and the thing which I count most on is the potential of this very young team. One of the youngest teams in the league."

But Iordanescu also took time to pay tribute to his predecessor.

"He [Dionisi] definitely worked hard," said Iordanescu.

"He did and left good things, very good things, already I saw many of them. But in football when things don't run the way you want and when the results are not backing up your work, it's difficult.

"I know he is a coach that put a lot of heart in his work and thank him for the good things that he did, and also tried to achieve here."

The task at hand now for Iordanescu is to succeed where Dionisi, and so many other Hornets bosses since their Premier League relegation in 2022, could not.

#761. 'Priceless' Duran proves 'the man' but is he papering over cracks at Celtic?

Camilo Duran's 15-goal haul this season has made him an invaluable player for a Celtic side fighting for European progression

"Duran is priceless for us at the moment".

It would be difficult for a football manager to muster up a higher compliment for one of his players - given he should know exactly how much he did cost - but Celtic boss Martin O'Neill was rightly effusive in his praise for Camilo Duran.

With 15 goals in 23 appearances, six assists, and another late European winner on Thursday, the Colombian was once again the main man for a struggling Celtic side.

His double against Besiktas breathed life into their Europa League campaign last time out, and his late leap to nod in the winner against Torreense kept it alive.

Duran, 24, started on the bench but was brought on with just over half an hour to go as O'Neill watched his side labour against a team currently 13th in the Portuguese second tier.

Celtic would still be searching for their first European win were it not for their summer arrival from Qarabag, whose goals have played a key part in keeping his team within touching distance of a play-off spot with three fixtures to play.

"He's taken on this mantle of being the man and he's been fantastic," said O'Neill, who started Duran on the bench. "We tried a similar approach against Besiktas.

"Sometimes by the time Duran gets subbed on, you could be behind. But I think that's the sign of a brilliant player, he'll do something.

"He's not a big guy but he's just a super footballer, a super, super footballer."

'He's priceless for us' - O'Neill on match winner Duran

Duran's summer arrival was overshadowed when, just over a fortnight later, a club-record fee was paid to Bodo Glimt for another striker, Kasper Hogh.

While recent weeks have been dominated by debates over Duran or Hogh, the debate now seems settled, with the Colombian operating on a different level from his striking counterpart.

Anyone watching Celtic in Portugal would have watched Hogh find space a handful of times in the area, but repeatedly fail to find a team-mate or trouble the goalkeeper. Duran didn't need to be asked twice.

"I don't know how many touches he got, but he had the telling touch," James McFadden said on Sportsound post-match.

Duran's goals have also proved decisive in securing domestic points against Falkirk and Hibernian, and with Celtic just a point clear of Rangers, he is indeed invaluable.

Despite his late header giving the thousands of travelling Celtic fans a thrilling end to a relatively turgid game, the intervention is another significant moment in a season that is threatening to unravel if individual performances fail to continue papering over glaring deficiencies across the park.

If the lively Jota - who lasted 74 minutes - was not creating chances, tormenting full-backs or digging out enticing crosses in the first half, Celtic seemed without any real plan of attack.

Yang and Luke McCowan's involvements were limited at best, Hogh's chance to stake a claim was sub-par to be kind, and there was no driving force from the middle of the park to show some impetus.

Arithmetically, Celtic can still finish in any position in the Europa League table. But if they are to claim a playoff or automatic qualification spot, they will need Duran to remain in such a rich vein of form.

Duran spares Celtic's blushes against Portuguese second-tier side Torreense

Celtic news, views and analysis all in one place

#760. Price out in Players Championship Finals first round in night of upsets

Report as Grand Slam champion Gerwyn Price, World No 2 Gian Van Veen, and No 1 seed Wessel Nijman all knocked out in first round at Players Championship Finals; watch the World Darts Championship at London's Alexandra Palace, live on Sky Sports from December 11-January 3

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Three of darts' biggest names were subject to shock upsets in the Players Championship Finals as Grand Slam champion Gerwyn Price, World No 2 Gian Van Veen, and No 1 seed Wessel Nijman were all knocked out in the first round at Minehead.

Price was beaten by 6-4 Sebastian Bialecki - the first time the Pole had beaten the Welshman in his career - while Jeffery de Graaf won two legs on the bounce to consign van Veen to defeat by the same scoreline.

Nijman was upset by 20-year-old Henry Coates despite posting an average of 110 - the second-highest average in Players Championship Finals history.

World No 4 Luke Humphries, meanwhile, battled through his recurring back injury to secure a routine 6-3 victory against Darryl Pilgrim, while Michael van Gerwen withstood Connor Scutt to secure safe passage with a 6-3 first-round win of his own.

Beau Greaves also progressed to the second round with a scrappy 6-3 victory against former Lakeside champion Christian Kist despite a mediocre average of 89.64, and will face Rob Owen in the next round.

Van Veen, Nijman and Price joined James Wade, Gary Anderson, and Rob Cross as six of the top 25 players in the world were eliminated at the first opportunity in the last major before the World Darts Championship, which is live on Sky Sports from December 11th.

Wade was beaten 6-4 by Justin Hood and 2014 winner Anderson slipped to a 6-4 loss against Karel Sedlacek, while Cross fell to a thrilling 6-5 loss to Mickey Mansell.

Van Veen - who finished runner-up to Price at the Grand Slam - struggled from the outset and throughout his match, managing only one maximum and checking out a lowly 15% of his finishes.

The Dutchman had three darts at double 16 to keep himself in the tournament, but failed to level the scores at 5-5 before de Graaf ruthlessly produced a 112 checkout to produce the first upset of the round.

Price, fresh off his first major win in four years after three successive final defeats, was heavily favoured against 22-year-old Bialecki, and looked to have rediscovered his tournament-winning form at the perfect moment when he produced a stunning 120 checkout to peg the deficit back to 5-4.

But Bialecki kept his cool and threw for the match, claiming his first career win against Price at the seventh attempt. The Pole will face off against de Graaf in round two.

The status quo was somewhat restored when Humphries and van Gerwen produced characteristically routine wins against lower-ranked opponents, with Humphries silencing doubters by averaging 93.32 in a week dominated by coverage of his injury.

But the show was stolen by Coates. The Derby native overcame his opponent's stellar average by notching an incredible 85.71% checkout success rate to claim victory in only his fourth-ever televised game.

Elsewhere, Stephen Bunting edged into the next round after beating German Max Hopp in a last-leg decider, while Kevin Doets averaged 107.34 in his win over Ritchie Edhouse and Chris Dobey came from behind to beat Mike De Decker 6-4.

Watch the World Darts Championship at London's Alexandra Palace, live on Sky Sports from December 11-January 3. Stream darts and more through NOW with no contract.

#759. Paige DeSorbo Goes Social Media Official With Boyfriend Joe D’Amelio

#758. Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports

According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.

This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful."

"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.

At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.

The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

#757. What makes or breaks a high press?

Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz spearhead Liverpool's press under Andoni Iraola

A good high press has been the basis for some of the most successful sides in modern football but a well-oiled pressing machine has many moving parts - all requiring close attention.

When an out-of-possession plan is implemented poorly, entire seasons can fall apart.

So, what determines whether a press works or fails? And how are the always-adapting Premier League teams exploiting high presses this season?

When a team decides to press, they must first establish their intention. This informs how the players act.

Speaking to DAZN Portugal, Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler was asked about whether a good press relied more on physicality or courage.

"When you want to press high you need the courage and mindset to do it. Our mindset is we press to score, we don't just press to win the ball back."

In coaching, clarity is key - particularly when it comes to creating alignment in the squad and Hurzeler is deliberate in simplifying big ideas when delivering messages to his players, a skill he practised as a radio pundit during the World Cup.

"[Punditry] helps you as a coach in that you have to summarise things in a short and easy way so that everyone understands," he said. "Football might get more complex but simplicity counts."

Hurzeler's "pressing to score" is a phrase that communicates many ideas in a memorable three words: intensity, being proactive, and immediate forward-thinking on winning the ball.

It also frames pressing in a way that makes it easy for attackers to buy into, in the form of goals.

"You want commitment from everyone on the pitch," Hurzeler explained.

"If just one has doubts, the whole press is gone."

The Red Bull school of coaching uses a similarly succinct phrase - "the last step" to address these ideas around intention, collectiveness and aggression.

Summarised by Tactx, whose coaches have worked under the Red Bull model, the last step refers to "players [being] coached to attack through the opponent, using the final step to lunge aggressively at the ball".

"This action commits the defender fully and is often the decisive moment that allows possession to be won."

Pressing to engage rather than just to close distances ensures the team in possession aren't given the time or space to play through otherwise half-hearted pressure.

Applying team-wide pressure, Newcastle make a strong tackle and win the ball.

This forces a turnover that puts Newcastle in a favourable attacking position.

When discussing how good or bad a team is at pressing, how much they run is often brought up. But the distance a team covers fails to paint the full picture when it comes to the effectiveness of a team's pressing strategy.

Liverpool's current boss Andoni Iraola was asked about how he interpreted physical data last year.

"It's not 'we run a lot, so we are good,' no," he said. "The high-speed running, the sprint speeds [matter for us] - not total distance covered.

"[Some] teams that do not run a lot get very good results because they have [their] way of playing."

Sprints matter more than distance covered for Iraola's side, who have clear ideas of how to press, looking to win the ball back through a sudden and intense pressure from familiar positions they are well prepared for.

If the conditions to implement this press aren't on, the wingers can be seen dropping off, forming a more compact defensive shape with the likes of Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz defending in a front two for longer periods of the match.

It's smart. Liverpool look to maximise the effectiveness of when they do press, with full commitment expected in each sprint, with players conserving their energy in moments a press is less likely to succeed.

With pressing being a front-footed idea, coaches may throw caution to the wind but this can leave them exposed in ways teams have become better at exploiting.

Hurzeler touched on the need for balance when pressing.

"I always say in certain moments you need to have the courage to take risk but you need to have the discipline to control the risk," he said.

For Brighton, this looks like certain players abandoning man-to-man marking when their respective attacker attempts to drag them into awkward positions.

Instead, Brighton will protect the centre of the pitch on top of their man-to-man principles which helps them stay compact.

In yellow, we can see the man-oriented defence of Brighton against Arsenal. The players highlighted in white are taking a more central position designed to protect dangerous areas of the pitch. This is an example of how impressive coaches are combining man-to-man pressing with zonal ideas

When the defending side aren't compact, spaces exist for the attacking side to target. When players step up to press, these gaps can arise in between the lines.

Again, Brighton manage to plug these gaps well by pressing hard, reducing the time opponents have to play passes into midfield, while also encouraging players to make vertical jumps up the pitch, covering players left by teammates who have pressed higher up the pitch.

As Declan Rice passes the ball backwards, Brighton's players press forward, locking on to the player in front of them

Chema Andres recognises that Bruno Guimaraes has been left unmarked in midfield so makes a vertical jump, closing him down, and ensuring Brighton remain compact

When teams lack vertical compactness - not pressing with enough intensity and without making the necessary steps up the pitch - the space left in midfield has been exploited by clever sides, such as Leeds.

In their 4-1 loss to Daniel Farke's men, Chelsea looked to press high, with attackers and midfielders running up the pitch to apply pressure.

But when the ball went back the other way, these same players struggled.

The idea behind playing over a team's press isn't always to make the ball stick at the feet of a target man, although this helps. Instead space is found in the gaps between the pressing side's lines.

Recognising when teammates are likely to win headers or clip the ball forwards, midfielders are able to turn and run in the direction the ball is heading in, positioned ready to win second balls in numbers.

By comparison, the pressing side's midfielders, having to apply forward pressure before turning around to track back are often slower to contest second balls.

Chelsea play a long goal-kick towards Leeds' back line. This forward pass brings with it the forward pressure of Chelsea's attackers and midfielders. The Leeds' defender heads it back, against the direction of Chelsea's press

Leeds' midfielders have oriented themselves well to form a net around where the ball may drop. The Chelsea midfielders and attackers, starting from further away and having to turn around, aren't well placed to contest for the loose ball

The same ideas are seen again. The Leeds' midfielder, under insufficient pressure, is able to play the ball forward quickly. This catches Chelsea's midfield line high up the pitch. Chelsea's Romeo Lavia has to turn before he can get back into position whilst Leeds attacking midfielders are closer to the ball, facing forwards

This allows Leeds to exploit the space between Chelsea's lines

By this point, it will be clear that pressing is influenced by countless variables but it is worth highlighting one final factor; teams need solutions when pressing with one fewer player than the attacking side.

This most obviously happens when the opposition goalkeeper is involved in build-up play.

Here, the team in possession have 11 options against the 10 pressing players.

Obvious solutions come in the form one of the forward attackers pressing a centre-back at an angle which usually forces them to pass it back to the goalkeeper.

At that point, the same pressing player will continue his run, now pressing the keeper.

By curving their run and pressing at an angle, the idea is that the keeper will struggle to pass it back to the now unmarked centre-back.

This is generally true but again, good teams have found smart solutions to access this player.

Charalampos Kostoulas first presses Gabriel Magalhaes, who passes the ball to his keeper, David Raya. Kostoulas then curves his run, blocking off Raya's pass back to Gabriel

One solution comes when the keeper passes the ball into a central player who then bounces the pass into the unmarked centre-back. This comes with risk given that the central player is usually marked. But sudden darts towards the ball can give them the time and space to play the bounce pass required.

Under some pressure, Rice darts towards the ball, gaining some separation from his marker. He gestures for the ball knowing he can play a first time pass to Gabriel who is unmarked

What happens instead is Raya, under immense pressure, defaults to playing long. His pass ends up out of play.

A riskier but more impressive solution is when the keeper is willing and able to avoid the opponents attempt to force him in one direction, instead playing the ball back the other way themselves.

Queens Park Rangers' Pierce Charles, on loan from Manchester City, has done this better than most in world football, and his quality was clearest against Swansea's excellent press.

By playing against the direction of Swansea's press, to his unmarked teammate, he was able to immediately disorganise their press.

QPR's right-sided defender passes the ball back to Charles. The Swansea striker, first pressing the defender, angles his body to discourage Charles from playing back to the unmarked player. He closes Charles down as he does this

Swansea's press is designed to force Charles to his left but he bravely plays back the other way

By finding the unmarked man on the other side in space, Swansea have to reorganise their defensive shape

Changes in how a team presses force teams to innovate their build-up play which in turn force teams to innovate in how they press. It's a cycle that spins at a blistering pace, especially in the Premier League.

Given the detailed analysis and constant adaptation, teams and coaches in 2026 can ill-afford to rest on their laurels.

#756. EFL preview: Happy Potters face struggling Hammers

Mark Robins (left) has Stoke where Scott Parker (right) would love to take West Ham

You've dug the de-icer and novelty jumpers out the back of the cupboard and within days a square of chocolate before breakfast will be socially acceptable again.

December is looming large, but you can be sure the season of goodwill does not extend to the English Football League.

There are furious battles raging at the top and bottom of the Championship, League One and League Two with more than a third of the campaign in the rear-view mirror and a huge month coming up which might just determine who will be on the naughty or nice list in 2027.

Here are five things to look out for across the EFL before the advent calendars are opened.

'Massive for both' - Saints and Boro revisit Spygate rivalry

If, as they say, seven days is a long time in football, then seven months feels like a lifetime.

In April, West Ham were trying to maintain a two-point cushion over Tottenham in the Premier League relegation scrap, while Stoke were careering down the Championship table. A run of one point from their final six matches saw them finish 17th.

On Saturday, they meet at the London Stadium (15:00 GMT) with the Potters 11 points and 11 places above the Hammers in this season's Championship standings.

Tuesday's defeat at Portsmouth means Scott Parker has taken just two points from four games since replacing Nuno Espirito Santo at the helm in east London, with his side now winless in six games.

The Hammers slipped into the bottom half of the table following Wednesday's results â the Irons have not finished lower than eighth in the second tier since 1956.

By contrast Mark Robins has led Stoke to five straight wins.

The 2-1 victory against Millwall on Wednesday means they have taken an incredible 35 points from their past 14 games, having begun the season with three straight losses.

A sixth win in a row might be enough to see Stoke take over at the top, given leaders Middlesbrough play at Southampton on Friday night, while a seventh game without a win could leave the Hammers closer to the relegation zone than the promotion places.

Unthinkable for the pre-season title favourites, and with six of their seven games before the turn of the year against sides scrapping for the automatic promotion spots or play-off places, this could just be the start of a bleak winter for the Irons.

As far as claret and blue teams freshly relegated from the Premier League go, West Ham have got it pretty good compared to Burnley.

Wednesday's 2-0 defeat by Birmingham at Turf Moor made it an English record 24 games without a home win, a run stretching back to October 2025.

Overall, the Clarets have won just one of their past 29 league games dating back to February - a 4-0 triumph at Watford on 10 October.

Fabio Celestini's side are second-bottom, a point above Derby, and could sink to the foot of the table if they fail to win at Millwall on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

Wednesday's 2-1 defeat at Stoke was a fourth straight defeat for Alex Neil's side who have taken just 12 points from their past 15 games, losing nine of them.

Pretty incredible seeing as how the Lions lost just 11 across the whole of last season, when they finished third, and might well have found themselves in the division above the Clarets this season, had things turned out differently in their play-off semi-final against Hull City.

Edward Iordanescu was in the stand for Watford's midweek home defeat by Blackburn

The game at The Den is not the only intriguing one in the second tier this Saturday as new basement-boys Derby welcome crisis club Watford to Pride Park (15:00 GMT).

The Rams have taken two steps back after taking one forward, picking up their only win in their past 13 games when they beat Bolton at home on 6 November.

They lost 2-0 to Southampton last weekend and 3-0 at Wolves on Tuesday in a game where they allowed 39 shots on their goal - the most by any side in the Championship in 11 years.

Preston North End's resurgence has left the Rams bottom of the pile with 35 goals conceded in 17 matches - the worst in the second tier along with Burnley.

They welcome a Hornets side who are 20th, three points above the drop-zone, after Wednesday's 1-0 home defeat to Blackburn, before which the players met new boss Edward Iordanescu for the first time.

The Romanian certainly has a big task on his hands, Watford have taken a single point from eight away games and were thumped 4-0 at Sheffield United last Saturday in Alessio Dionisi's last stand, while they now haven't scored in three games overall.

We are going to find out an awful lot about Sheffield Wednesday's prospects in League One in the next three weeks.

Dave Challinor's arrival has seemingly steadied the ship, but a stalemate at Stevenage on Tuesday was a sideways step after back-to-back wins over Plymouth and Barnsley in which Wednesday rode their luck at times.

The Owls are fourth, five points off the top, and unbeaten in five, but have played a game more than most sides around them and face in-form promotion rivals Oxford United, Leicester and Luton in the run-up to Christmas after Saturday's visit of Reading (15:00 GMT).

The Royals have slipped to ninth after a run of one point from a possible 12, losing their past three and taking only six points from eight away games, with just one win.

They will be desperate to return to the play-off race and end their slump, and if they can do it the pressure will be firmly on Wednesday in the weeks to come.

In the past 14 seasons they have been promoted or relegated in 10 of them, but Millers fans will be keen for just a season of stability given the way things have started following the drop from League One last season.

An eight-match winless run has left Alex Bruce's Millers second-bottom, only off the foot of the EFL by virtue of scoring more than Crawley, level on points and goal difference - pretty incredible for a club which has spent more seasons in the Championship (seven) than anywhere else since they were last in the fourth tier in 2013.

They will seek to end their slide with Bruce sat in the stands on Saturday (15:00 GMT) when they host Oldham, a side who were mid-table in the National League when the Millers began their last Championship campaign, but now sit three points better off in 20th.

Rotherham actually picked up a creditable goalless draw at Grimsby last weekend, which denied the Mariners a place in the automatic promotion spots.

Fourth-placed Town will seek to put that right when they head to Crewe, two places behind on goal difference alone, this weekend, in a crazy division where just four points separate Grimsby from Fleetwood in 15th.

You can follow the entire EFL weekend as it happens here on the BBC Sport website and app, starting with live text coverage of Southampton v Middlesbrough on Friday, 27 November.
