#719. Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Rare Photos of Son Christopher on Thanksgiving

Billy Ray Cyrus celebrated Thanksgiving surrounded by family, including his rarely seen son Christopher Cody Cyrus, his wife Nicole and their baby Hudson.

Billy Ray Cyrus is celebrating in the heart of family.

The 65-year-old proved his heart is anything but achy breaky as he and partner Elizabethy Hurley enjoyed a blended Thanksgiving with their loved ones, including a rare appearance from Billy Ray’s son Christopher Cody Cyrus, whom the singer welcomed with ex-girlfriend Kristin Luckey.

“Happy Thanksgiving!” Billy Ray captioned his Nov. 26 Instagram carousel. “I am so thankful for this moment - grateful for this time with my incredible son Cody, his amazing wife Nicole and my beautiful grandson Hudson. Feeling truly blessed.”

In fact, Billy Ray was all smiles as he posed alongside Cody and the 34-year-old’s wife and baby in a restaurant. Also featured in the snaps were Elizabeth and her son Damian Charles Hurley, 24, the latter of whom cuddled baby Hudson close in one photo.

Damian, born in England to Elizabeth and American filmmaker Steve Bing, also leaned into the Turkey Day festivities, sharing Billy Ray’s post to his own Story and writing, “Happy Thanksgiving!”

As for Cody, while he leads a far more private life then many of his Cyrus siblings—Billy Ray also adopted Tish Cyrus’ kids Brandi Cyrus, 39, and Trace Cyrus, 37, during their marriage, in addition to the pair welcoming Miley Cyrus, 34, Braison Cyrus, 32, and Noah Cyrus, 26—he did attend Miley’s nuptials to Maxx Morando on Nov. 21.

In fact, Cody was among the Cyrus family members featured in Billy Ray’s photo carousel from the wedding, with the country singer raving over the family affair.

“My little girl married the love of her life! I can’t describe how beautiful it felt to have all my family together in one room, united by love,” he captioned his Nov. 24 post. “@miley words can’t begin to express how proud you make me every day… I’m the proudest dad alive!!”

The Hannah Montana alum also reserved some special words for his now son-in-law.

“@mmaxxm I’m so honored to welcome you to the family,” Billy Ray continued. “The two of you kids are a match made in heaven… Happy, happy birthday Miley - I can’t wait to keep celebrating you both today and forever!”

For a closer look at how Cody fits into the larger Cyrus family tree, read on.

Billy Ray Cyrus married Tish Cyrus (née Leticia Finley) on Dec. 28, 2003.

At the time they already shared 12-month-old daughter Destiny Hope Cyrus—you may know her as Miley Cyrus—and Tish was pregnant with their son Braison Cyrus, who was born May 9, 1994.

Seven months before Miley was born on Nov. 23, 1992, Billy Ray's ex-girlfriend Kristin Luckey gave birth to their son Christopher Cody Cyrus on April 8.

When the "Achy Breaky Heart" singer married Tish, he adopted her daughter Brandi Cyrus (born May 26, 1987) and son Trace Cyrus (Feb. 24, 1989), whose biological father is their mom's ex-husband Baxter Helson.

Tish and Billy Ray's youngest, daughter Noah Cyrus, was born Jan. 8, 2000.

From 2006 to 2010, Billy Ray played the father of Miley's normal-kid-who-moonlights-as-a-pop-star character in the Disney Channel sitcom Hannah Montana and a 2009 film adaptation.

While the Cyrus family was still based in Nashville, Billy Ray and Miley made the move to L.A. to jumpstart her own entertainment career.

Billy Ray and Tish announced in October 2010 that they were getting divorced, but by the following year were back together.

They filed for divorce again in June 2013 but reconsidered barely a month later, telling E! News at the time that they'd been to couple's counseling and it had done wonders for them.

But before they reconciled, when the news broke that her dad had made the first move in a Nashville court to end his marriage after 19 years, Miley tweeted, "@billyraycyrus since your text and email obviously aren't working would you like to talk like this?"

After starring in 2010's The Last Song together and dating off and on for a decade, Miley and Liam Hemsworth married in December 2018, not long after their Malibu home burned down.

The decision came "from a place of trauma and just trying to rebuild as quickly as we could," Miley recalled on her "Used to Be Young" TikTok series.

But Liam filed for divorce in August 2019 and they finalized the paperwork in January 2020.

"It's honestly very simple," a source told E! at the time. "They fell in love when they were young and they are just different people now."

Braison and his wife Stella Cyrus welcomed son Bear Chance Cyrus on June 8, 2021.

Tish filed for divorce fo a third time in April 2022, and this time it stuck.

Moreover, her petition citing "irreconcilable differences" noted that she and her husband of almost 30 years hadn't lived together since February 2020.

"It is after 30 years, five amazing children and a lifetime of memories, we have decided to go our separate ways—not with sadness, but with love in our hearts," Tish and Billy Ray told People in a statement. "We have grown up together, raised a family we can be so proud of, and it is now time to create our own paths."

The exes noted that they hadn't come to the decision to split up for good "lightly or quickly," adding, "We will always be family and look forward to a continued and loving shared experience as friends and parents."

Billy Ray quietly got engaged to Australian singer Firerose, who's 27 years his junior, in August 2022 but waited to confirm the news until that November.

"Growing up in Australia, my love of music was predominant over everything," Firerose told People. "I've known his music since forever."

What started as a friendship turned into more during the darkest days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

"All of the sudden, the life that I've always known as a touring artist didn't exist anymore," Billy Ray said. "A moment of so much change. And at the same time, Firerose, who had been such a light of positivity, such a best friend. And then when we began sharing the music, it just evolved more into, as musical soulmates, to soulmates, happy, pure love that to me, I didn't know could exist."

Around the time her ex-husband confirmed his engagment in November 2022, Tish went Instagram-official with Prison Break actor Dominic Purcell.

They got engaged in April 2023 and tied the knot that August in Malibu at sunset with Miley, Trace and Brandi all standing by their mom's side.

"Life is unpredictable & always full of changes," Trace captioned a photo of himself and two of his sibling with the bride. "I think the most important thing to do is cherish the past, look forward to the future, & always be happy in the present moment because that’s really all we have."

"To see my mom this happy and in love is very emotional for me," Miley told Vogue ahead of her mom's wedding. "Dom and my mom share the sweetest, most genuine love. It's almost like it's for the first time, which is so fitting for my mom who is such a young soul."

As for her dad's next chapter, however, a source close to Miley told E! News in October 2022 that she wasn't in love with it and didn't have a relationship with her future stepmom.

"The divorce between her parents put a strain on her relationship with her dad and it's been hard to connect with him in the last year," the source said. "She hopes they can eventually work on their relationship."

Billy Ray told People that November, however, that his family had "no hard feelings" about his engagement.

"Everybody's turning the page," he said. "It's been a lot, but everyone knew that it was time for a change."

He and Firerose got married on Oct. 10, 2023, calling it the "beautiful, joyous day that our two souls united as one in holy matrimony."

Only Some of Miley's Family Get Their Flowers

Whatever rift opened up between Miley and her dad apparently hadn't been repaired by the night of the 2024 Grammys on Feb. 4.

Tish and Brandi were there, as was Miley's boyfriend Maxx Morando, and they all got shout-outs when the "Flowers" singer won Record of the Year.

As Miley concluded her speech, "I don't think I forgot anyone."

None of the three officially confirmed or denied eyebrow-raising reports that Noah was involved with Dominic before her mother was, but the Grammy-nominated singer had some choice words for an Instagram commenter in April 2024 after the person crudely suggested that Noah and Tish both had "sexy time" with the actor.

"I'm so sorry but will you pleeeeeass just choke on the fattest c--k," Noah wrote in response. "Just for a lil bit. Great thanks."

Barely eight months after they tied the knot, Billy Ray filed to annul the union, alleging in court documents the marriage was "obtained by fraud."

He listed May 22, 2024, as their date of separation.

However, Billy Ray amended his plan and filed for divorce, which was settled that August.

"This has been absolutely the most crazy insane scam I have ever heard of," Billy Ray said in a statement to E! News. "Let alone the fact I'm right in the center and basically the target of the scheme. It's unfortunate it played out this way."

“Since my earliest memories all I can remember is being obsessed with you and thinking you were the coolest person ever," Trace began a Jan. 22, 2025, Instagram post directed at his father. "I wanted to be just like you. The day you adopted me was the happiest day of my life. Sadly the man that I wanted so desperately to be just like I barely recognize now."

Referring to his sisters, he continued, "Me and the girls have been genuinely worried about you for years but you’ve pushed all of us away."

Noah was especially hurt, according to Trace.

"Noah desperately has wanted you to be a part of her life and you haven't even been there for her," he wrote. "That’s your baby girl. She deserves better. Somehow just like me she still idolizes you though. We are all hanging on to memories of the man we once knew & hoping for the day he returns."

After his son Trace said he and his sisters—including Miley, Brandi and Noah—were worried about Billy Ray, the country music star wrote in the caption of a YouTube Shorts post on Jan. 26, 2025. “Praying for my family. For my children … sons and daughters…and their mother."

In March 2025, Billy Ray seemed to signal that his bond with his kids was improving as he shared a touching tribute to Miley and Noah in honor of their latest music projects.

“Flesh and blood … completely taking their art to a whole new level. Congratulations girls,” he wrote on Instagram at the time. “I’m so damn proud of both of you. I’m actually crying as I write this. Thank God you can’t see me.”

In May 2025, Billy Ray shared a photo of himself with Miley, her boyfriend Maxx Morando and his son Braison Cyrus at what appears to be the "Achy Breaky Heart" singer's farm in Tennessee. He captioned his Instagram post, “Happy Birthday Braison!!!!!"

One day later, Miley broke her silence about the family rift rumors, noting on Instamgram that she and her dad "have had our challenges over the years."

Miley continued, "Now, in my thirties, family is my priority above all else. I'm at peace knowing bridges have been built and time has done a lot of healing. Grateful for the good health and love that flows through my family."

#718. Gibbs-White stars, Fofana struggles - player ratings for Forest v Chelsea

Premier League highlights: Nottingham Forest 3-2 Chelsea

Morgan Gibbs-White scored twice as Nottingham Forest beat Chelsea at the City Ground for the first time since 1997.

Igor Jesus' brilliant volley opened the scoring after just five minutes, before Gibbs-White struck twice in the second half as Chelsea were consigned to a fourth defeat in five matches.

Forest ran out 3-2 winners despite Emmanuel Emegha twice pulling goals back.

Here's how I rated the players and how you rated the players.

Matz Sels: The Belgian goalkeeper could do little about Emegha's goals but did not need to make many saves. 6

Jair Cunha: Cunha made one brilliant last-ditch tackle in the second half as Chelsea pushed for an equaliser. 7

Nikola Milenkovic: The Serbian was solid in the middle of the back three but otherwise unremarkable. 7

Murillo: The Brazilian centre-back made a host of important tackles and no-nonsense clearances throughout. He set the tone for a physical display and had a powerful volley saved. 7

Daniel Munoz: A typically energetic presence on the right, he also set up the opening goal. 7

James McAtee: The midfielder was good in possession but his shots lacked threat. His set-piece delivery was also poor. He did, however, win a few fouls for his team to take the pressure off. 7

Xaver Schlager: The combative midfielder set the tone early by winning the ball back in Chelsea's half on multiple occasions. He screened the backline well as Chelsea pushed for an equaliser. His wonderful pass through the eye of the needle created Forest's third. 9

Neco Williams: The Welshman battled hard with Pedro Neto in a tactical contest that ended with both players emerging with credit. 7

Igor Jesus: His sensational first-time volley opened the scoring just five minutes into the match, while the rest of his play was neat and tidy. 8

Morgan Gibbs-White: The forward scored his first goal in 11 games against Chelsea from the penalty spot in the second half. He took that chance and then another when played through by Schlager. 8

Liam Delap: The former Chelsea striker proved his worth to Forest by leading the line brilliantly, carrying a threat, looking dangerous in transition and ultimately winning a penalty for his side. 8

Subs not used: John Victor, Netz, Diomande, Yates, Hudson-Odoi, Kalimuendo

Chelsea have now lost four of their past five games

Emiliano Martinez: The Argentine goalkeeper was sent the wrong way from the spot and could not have saved Jesus' volley but made a couple of other saves. 6

Josh Acheampong: The young defender played within himself at the City Ground. 5

Wesley Fofana: The Frenchman was booed by his own supporters and told he is "not welcome here". It was a tough end to a horrible week which only got worse as he gave away the penalty having first been caught under a long ball. He was substituted in the 56th minute while also on a yellow card. 3

Moises Caicedo: A shock selection to start at centre-back for first time in his 210 games in English football, the Ecuadorian looked out of sorts with possession and in his positioning. He failed to cover for Fofana before he gave away the penalty. 5

Pep Chavarria: The Spanish full-back was an anonymous presence but did not make any obvious mistakes. 5

Romeo Lavia: The Belgian recovered from a poor touch early on to set the tempo for possession domination and his passes had real purpose. 7

Jordan Henderson: The 36-year-old was one of the weaker Chelsea performers as he filled in for now-defender Caicedo. 5

Pedro Neto: The Portuguese winger showed impressive work-rate competing with Williams, while threatened with his running in behind. His second-half shot was blocked but led to Chelsea's first goal, while his cross set up his side's second. 7

Cole Palmer: The forward was creative and highly involved for Chelsea but could not deliver that moment. It owed more to his team-mates not performing than himself. 6

Morgan Rogers: Rogers squandered multiple chances, including a huge opportunity to equalise from a corner midway through the second half. 4

Danny Welbeck: The 35-year-old striker had absolutely no service but was also completely anonymous in the first half and was taken off at the interval. 4

Emmanuel Emegha (on 45, Welbeck): An outstanding second-half display, with a brilliant touch and shot to pull one after the ball deflected into his path. He headed in a second at the far post. It raises the question about why he did not start having also scored against Leeds last weekend. 8

Levi Colwill (on 56, Fofana): The England international will be frustrated to have been dropped for a midfielder but was forced on amid Fofana's struggles and did not have much chance to shine. 5

Subs not used: Penders, Gusto, Barco, Nicoll-Jazuli, Estevao

After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users.

#716. Orangutans face bleak future after Indonesia’s devastating wildfires

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

An orangutan affected by smoke inhalation receives emergency oxygen.Credit: REUTERS/Willy Kurniawan

For most of October, parts of Indonesia felt dystopian as wildfires turned the sky a reddish orange.

“It felt like you were on Mars,” says Erin Vogel, a primatologist at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey.

Vogel was visiting the Tuanan Orangutan Research Station in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, at the time. She and her colleagues have been conducting research on the critically endangered Bornean orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) there for more than 20 years, but this trip she spent much of her time fighting fires. There were roughly 300,000 blazes in the region between July and October, and October’s level of toxic particulate matter in the air was roughly 400 times higher than what the World Health Organization deems safe.

Indonesia is experiencing one of its most severe fire and haze season of the past three decades, in part because a super El Niño has dried out vegetation and brought winds that fuelled the flames. More than 2.8 million hectares have burnt across Indonesia so far, and Kalimantan has been affected the worst. Fires devoured 60% of Bornean orangutans’ habitats in Kalimantan, including healthy forests such as those at the Tuanan research station and in Gunung Palung National Park.

Nature spoke to Vogel about the disaster and what it means for orangutans. At the time of the interview, fires were still smouldering in Tuanan peat swamp forests.

It was depressing and horrid. I’ve never seen so much forest loss in the 23 years I have worked in Indonesia. In the sky, there was this orange-brown haze that was very thick and it burnt your lungs if you weren’t wearing a respirator.

When I arrived in Tuanan, it really struck me how quiet the forests had become. You didn’t hear birds; you didn’t hear insects; you didn’t hear anything except trees burning and falling.

The forest staff, the orangutan staff, the phenology staff and the fire teams were all fighting fires. I felt in awe of those heroes voluntarily fighting these fires day and night. They’d all been doing so for more than two months straight. It takes real strength to be able to do that and not give up, and our team is just so positive and hopeful.

We saw some orangutans who seemed to be very lethargic and sick. We came across one of the males we’ve been studying for more than 15 years, and he was on the ground, breathing heavily. But when we saw him a couple of days later, he seemed to have recovered a little bit. He was near the research station, eating some vegetation on the ground, climbing trees and eating fruits. That reassures us that he is doing better.

We’re seeing orangutans being displaced from one area to others. That means we’re going to have competition between individuals over limited resources. That’s also going to change their behaviour. It’s going to be interesting to see what happens.

#714. Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience

The US is now officially a measles contagion zone. By mid-2026, there were more infections than in all of the previous year. But the country could beat measles again, just like Brazil did two years ago.

Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.

Four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) said the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.

Look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.

In 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.

Brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.

Brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected measles case. Here's Brazil's own rule:

It has also made hunting for cases a national habit. In a program called "Dia S," health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.

Brazil also holds mass vaccination days called "Dia D." There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.

If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and vaccinate them and other people living nearby.

The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious. A country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.

"Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

The US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on new vaccination recommendations for children in August 2026. It came at a time, when, as we reported, experts said people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. But like PAHO's Barbosa said, neglecting vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

To be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

Before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners in the US unprotected.

In the Texas counties where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved.

But vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.

To prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

And the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak is likely to start.

Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.

But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.

Data from Europe shows that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.

Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.

In Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.

But in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

The Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as by November in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.

Measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

It's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.

But it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

#713. Wilshere v Ramsey - Arsenal legends treading similar managerial paths

Jack Wilshere and Aaron Ramsey are the third and fourth youngest managers across the 92 Premier League and EFL clubs

Aaron Ramsey and Jack Wilshere have a lot in common.

Both were midfield prodigies. Both won the FA Cup playing for Arsenal under Arsene Wenger. Both represented their countries.

The image of the pair celebrating Ramsey's extra-time winner together in the 2014 FA Cup final against Hull City to end Arsenal's nine-year trophy drought at the time will forever be ingrained in the north London club's history.

They were teenagers when they made their Premier League debuts for the Gunners on the same day just two minutes apart as substitutes in a 4-0 win at Blackburn in September 2008.

Aged just 16 and 17, each were considered hot prospects who would go on to have excellent careers - and so it proved in many ways, even if both were restricted by injuries along the way.

Now 34 and 35, their paths cross again under different circumstances but many similarities very much still remain.

They are both in League One in their first permanent managerial jobs. And, guess what? Both their sides are in fine form and vying for promotion to the Championship.

It will be the first time they have met as permanent managers when Wilshere's Luton Town host Ramsey's Oxford United at Kenilworth Road on Saturday (15:00 GMT).

Jack Wilshere won two FA Cups with Arsenal and Aaron Ramsey won three

Ramsey and Wilshere have both tried to play down their reunion.

"Obviously it will be nice to see Jack again, but it's not about us," Ramsey told BBC Radio Oxford.

Except it is about them a little bit, given their 101 appearances in 10 years together in the Arsenal midfield - and as two young managers who are following almost identical paths.

Immediately after retiring from playing in July 2022, Wilshere was appointed the under-18s head coach at Arsenal, the club where he had risen from the youth academy to the first team.

Meanwhile, former Wales international Ramsey gained coaching experience towards the end of his playing career, also working with the under-18s at boyhood club Cardiff City.

Wilshere joined Norwich City as a coach for the 2024-25 season and it was at the end of that campaign he would first meet Ramsey as a manager in a remarkable twist of fate after they were both placed in interim charge of the Canaries and Bluebirds respectively.

The bragging rights went to Wilshere on that day in May last year as Norwich beat Cardiff 4-2.

Despite their close relationship and working towards the same objectives in the same league, they have not spoken "for a while".

"We are in a similar position at the moment, but I haven't had much dialogue with him over the last few months," said Ramsey.

"We're both fighting for the same things but, for me, it's just going out there to try and win a game of football."

"It doesn't change anything for how we prepare," Wilshere told BBC Three Counties Radio on Friday.

"Of course, when I see Aaron, that'll be a nice moment. We spent a lot of good times together.

"He's had a really good start and credit to him. He's got a football brain, he's got a good career in the game and he's clearly taking that into his coaching.

Only joint-leaders Stockport and Huddersfield have scored more goals than Luton (29) this season, while Oxford boast the third-best defensive record

Since taking over at Luton in October 2025, Wilshere has already tasted silverware, lifting the EFL Trophy at Wembley in April - a feeling he said he enjoyed more as a manager than when he was a player.

The 34-year-old guided the Hatters to seventh in League One last season, narrowly missing out on a play-off spot by a point.

Wilshere slightly edges his counterpart in terms of managerial experience, with 64 games in all competitions as Luton boss, while Ramsey has taken charge of 18 matches in his first season with the U's.

Neither could have their side in much better shape heading into Saturday's showdown.

After a stuttering start to 2026-27, Luton have won five of their past six games (D1) to climb from 16th up to fifth.

As for Ramsey, he is doing a fine job with Oxford considering the club have been under a transfer embargo since he arrived - and says he is "loving every second of it".

His side are on an 11-game unbeaten run - the second-longest across the entire Football League behind only Salford City (13).

With just one defeat so far, Oxford are third and three points behind Stockport and Huddersfield with two games in hand.

Oxford could go top of League One if they win their two games in hand on Stockport and Huddersfield

The influences on Wilshere and Ramsey are clear to see, both in the styles of play they adopt and the way they conduct themselves.

They have both learnt from the same mentors, particularly Wenger and current Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta, who they also played alongside in midfield.

It is perhaps no surprise the pair have gone into coaching - a common theme among Wenger's disciples.

Arteta, Patrick Vieira, Thierry Henry, Ashley Cole, Robin van Persie, Kolo Toure and Cesc Fabregas have also done so.

Wilshere and Ramsey have both spoken openly about the huge impact Wenger has had on them.

Ramsey scored 58 goals and made 329 appearances for Arsenal under Arsene Wenger

They also give a lot of credit to their role model Arteta.

Watching from afar, Ramsey previously said it was inspiring to see his former team-mate guide Arsenal to the Premier League title and Champions League final.

It was also Arteta who advised Ramsey to take his coaching badges and has continued to help him along the way.

But for Wilshere, he got to learn first hand from the Spaniard on the training ground.

"I got to see Mikel and how he coached and the influence he was having," Wilshere said last month.

"I would ask him questions, why he's doing certain things, and I started to fall in love with it and how he started to prepare training sessions.

"I was influenced by Mikel, but then I had to learn how to teach. I had to learn how to get that across, how to plan a session and how to get the outcomes that you wanted."

Mikel Arteta and Wilshere played together 53 times for Arsenal

There are some key ideologies Wilshere and Ramsey share which might sound familiar - an emphasis on a high-technical level, possession-based football, hard work and intensity.

Wilshere encourages his team to get the ball to his best attacking players but is maybe Arteta-coded with his focus on "winning duels, second balls and competing physically".

He also sometimes allows his full-backs freedom - something else Arteta is renowned for at Arsenal to create unpredictability.

It is not just on the pitch where Wilshere takes care of the details.

When he walked into his post-match press conference at Wembley after winning his first trophy as a boss last season, he shook the hand of every reporter in the room - a small insight into his warm nature.

The ex-England international has also spoken about how he expresses both empathy and honesty with his players.

Wilshere started his career at Luton's youth academy before moving to Arsenal

Ramsey made no bones about his plans when he joined Oxford in June either.

"I have a really clear way of playing, an identity that I want to create," he said at the time. "But that is built on clear principles first, underpinned by elite habits and behaviours."

That identity so far has been a team that likes to play out from the back, dominate possession and attack with verve.

Only Leicester (66%) and Stockport (62%) have had a higher average share of possession than Oxford (57%) in League One so far this season.

"I think it's evident to see why we're doing it," said Ramsey, who wants his team to take risks.

"It's not always going to be perfect. We're fully aware of that but those bits in the game where we can carve teams open - that outweighs the rest."

That approach sounds very Wenger-esque, with a sprinkling of Arteta when it comes to mindset and tweaking their tactics to suit the game on offer.

"Every week is different," he said. "But what I've liked so much about us is that we've always been able to adapt and figure out what's going on and ultimately win games of football."

Ramsey also exudes calm on the touchline, another trait perhaps borrowed from his former French boss.

Ramsey 'loving every second' of being Oxford boss

Learning from Arteta and inspiring youngsters - Wilshere on management

Back to the immediate matters in hand this weekend, and it could be a pivotal one.

"Some are talking about this game, when you put aside the Arsenal connections, as season-defining in League One," said BBC Radio Oxford sports presenter Jerome Sale.

Ramsey was keen to reiterate that this game was not about him and Wilshere.

"Far from it," he added. "It's about the players. Two good teams going head-to-head and hopefully everything on the pitch does the talking."

#712. Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust

When humans live on the moon, we'll need to grow food on the moon, too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon.

To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal.

"We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement. "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon."

To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith, the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions.

The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil.

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement.

The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth.

Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

#711. JoJo Siwa and Chris Hughes Break Up After 1.5 Years of Dating

JoJo Siwa and Chris Hughes, who met while competing on Celebrity Big Brother UK in 2025, split over one year into their relationship, multiple outlets confirmed.

The "Karma" singer has split from former Love Island UK star Chris Hughes after a year and a half together, multiple outlets confirmed.

E! News reached out to reps for the pair for comment but has not yet heard back.

Siwa, 23, and Hughes, 33, first met in 2025 on the set of Celebrity Big Brother UK. While the Dance Moms alum was dating podcaster Kath Ebbs at the time, she formed a close bond with Hughes during the reality competition series.

"I've always told myself I'm a lesbian and I think being here, I’ve realized: ‘Oh, I’m not a lesbian, I’m queer,'" she told housemate Danny Beard at the time. "And I think that’s really cool."

Siwa broke up from Ebbs shortly after the show's finale in May, with her and Hughes going public with their romance the following month.

“It’s not platonic anymore,” Siwa admitted in a June 2025 interview with The Guardian, “and it’s been a beautiful development, a beautiful connection, and I’m absolutely head over heels for him and he’s the same way.”

The "Boomerang" artist also clarified her sexuality, emphasizing that she still considers herself to be a proud member of the LGBTQ+ community.

"I think the most beautiful term now is queer,” Siwa told E! News that same month. "There's loads of beautiful, different sexualities. Sexuality and queerness is a lovely rainbow that has all different places, and it also has places on this rainbow that we don't even know exist yet.”

She continued, "What I realized with Christopher is I never have second guessed my feelings for him. Therefore, I've never second guessed my happiness, I've never second guessed what I'm feeling. And I think that's the most beautiful thing.”

#710. 'You're not welcome here' - Chelsea fans turn on Fofana

Premier League highlights: Nottingham Forest 3-2 Chelsea

Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana was subjected to repeated boos and told "you're not welcome here" by his own fans during Friday's Premier League defeat by Nottingham Forest.

The jeers aimed at the 25-year-old were heard every time he touched the ball and came after an unauthorised interview with French YouTuber Zach Nani was released.

In that controversial two-hour conversation, Fofana also appeared to joke about missing his penalty during last month's Carabao Cup shootout defeat by Liverpool.

Manager Xabi Alonso said the French centre-back had apologised and "it won't be repeated".

But Fofana endured a difficult time in his side's trip to Forest as supporters made their feelings known.

After Chelsea went behind to a brilliant volley from Igor Jesus in the fifth minute, Fofana also conceded a penalty for the home side's second goal from Morgan Gibbs-White in the 51st minute.

He was booked for the foul on Liam Delap in the box, and then replaced by Levi Colwill in the 56th minute - just after Emmanuel Emegha had pulled a goal back for the visitors - before Gibbs-White made it 3-1 in the 72nd minute.

Emegha scored again in the 89th minute to make it 3-2, but Forest held on to secure their first win over Chelsea at the City Ground since 1997.

Alonso defended Fofana after the game and said in his post-match news conference: "We have to stick together, and everyone that is in the changing room, everyone in the team is needed.

"We need to help, and we need to go through these tough moments all together, and we don't leave anyone apart.

"We need to support everyone. That is because we need everyone, and we need the fans.

"We need all the players. We need to stick together because if not, things will get more complicated, and that's what we want to do."

Asked whether the reaction of the Chelsea fans will make it difficult to pick Fofana going forward, he added: "Well, I'm thinking right after the game, and for the next games, we will see."

Wesley Fofana has made 10 appearances for Chelsea this season

Meanwhile, Nani has moved to defend Fofana, saying the player was "clearly" not happy during the interview and admitted he had to perform better.

Fofana also explained he opted to take a penalty against Liverpool as one of the senior players on the pitch, having joined in a Â£75m move from Leicester City in 2022.

But he confessed football had reached a stage where he was "more unhappy than happy", before recovering physically and mentally.

The release of the interview has coincided with the club's poor run of form, with Chelsea losing 4-1 at home to Leeds United last weekend to make it three defeats in four matches.

The defence, in particular, has come in for criticism, with the Blues one of four clubs to have conceded more than 20 goals in the Premier League after 11 matches.

Having been subjected to racist abuse in the past, Fofana spoke about handling comments during a club-organised interview on this summer's pre-season tour of Asia.

He is understood to be one of the highest earners at Stamford Bridge.

#707. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

#706. How JoJo Siwa and Chris Hughes’ Romance Unraveled After 1.5 Years

After JoJo Siwa and Chris Hughes fell in love on Celebrity Big Brother, their relationship was unable to stand the test of time, ending a year and a half later.

JoJo Siwa has long danced to the beat of her own drum, and she’s back to doing it alone.

While Siwa came out as a lesbian in 2023 after previously describing herself as pansexual, the Dance Moms alum proved sexuality can be an ever-evolving spectrum when she revealed she and British reality star Chris Hughes had fallen in love.

What began as a close bond while filming Celebrity Big Brother in the UK soon turned into something more after the season wrapped in the spring of 2025, as the pair confirmed their romance that May.

In the time since, Siwa reflected on how meeting Hughes changed what she thought she’d understood about her sexuality, having “always been grossed out by dudes.”

“Chris is a very conventionally hot dude,” she explained on the Wildmen podcast in September. “[But] I thought [he] was just another friend. Once I realized that I wasn't grossed out by the thought of him being a boy, I was like, ‘Whoa.’ It was weird because I'd never thought that before.”

In fact, as she’d never felt a spark for her “conventionally hot” male friends, Siwa was taken aback when her feelings for Hughes began to trend towards the romantic in the Big Brother house, admitting, “I just never thought it was possible.”

And though she also noted Hughes was “very much so the special dude” that could break her previous assumptions about her sexuality, Siwa has also been candid about how previously labeling herself as lesbian never quite felt right.

"I did that because of the pressure," Siwa—who dated Kylie Prew, Avery Cyrus and Kath Ebbs prior to Hughes—told the Daily Mail in 2025. “You just get put in this world where you feel like, because you now have said, 'Oh, I'm a lesbian,' you have to be a lesbian."

But everything changed after meeting Hughes, with the pair both raving about their connection.

“I feel so relaxed and at ease with where I'm at,” Siwa told E! News in July 2025. “I feel so happy and peaceful that the love that I feel is so real. You can't really help who you fall in love with.”

And the feeling was more than mutual, with Hughes telling E! that same month, “She's literally the love of my life, but she's also my best friend. Like, we sit and do nothing together."

And with hopes expressed for future babies and rings given at Christmastime in the months after, it seemed like Siwa and Hughes were in it for the long haul.

That is until Nov. 2026, when their breakup was confirmed by multiple outlets.

Though neither Hughes nor Siwa shared additional insight into their split in the immediate wake of the news, the breakup came as a shock to fans.

After all, just days earlier Siwa confirmed “having a baby” was at the top of her personal agenda during an appearance on the Petticoats Revolution podcast.

“Obviously that's not a career thing,” she continued, “but like a life thing.”

Now, however, it would appear Siwa will need to look elsewhere to start that next chapter.

For a complete look back at Siwa and Hughes’ road to romance, and their abrupt end, read on.

The couple's whirlwind romance unfolded for the whole world to see during their appearance on Celebrity Big Brother.

A year later, Siwa—who split from ex Kath Ebbs following her time on the U.K. the series—released the song "Serendipity" in honor of the now-couple's chance encounter.

"The only word to explain what happened on this day a year ago… Serendipity," Siwa wrote in an Instagram post. "Today, I’m reminded of the moment that quietly changed everything."

Less than a month after they put their bond on display in the Big Brother house and emphasizing they were just friends, Hughes and Siwa confirmed they were dating in late May 2025.

At the time, Siwa cheekily nodded at the romance during a cover of "Bette Davis Eyes" at one of her shows, in which she instead sang "Chris Hughes' eyes."

The Love Island alum joined Siwa at several stops of her Infinity Heart Tour, which spanned across Europe, the U.K. and the United States. In a sweet glimpse at their backstage moments, Siwa added of the tour in an Instagram post, "The show represents who I want to be as a person and the artist that I wanna be in this lifetime, and it’s translated so well to the crowd."

Siwa and Hughes stepped out for their first red carpet as a couple at the Dancers Against Cancer's 2025 Gala of the Stars in Beverly Hills, California.

Siwa shared a glimpse into the couple's favorite bonding activity: golfing in a sweet Instagram photo dump of her summertime adventures.

In September 2026, Hughes gave his followers a slice of life moment by filming Siwa arriving to his place in England—and naturally they shared a sweet embrace to boot.

October 2026: Coming Back Like a Boomerang

Siwa and Hughes turned the Gala of the Stars into a date night two years in a row by attending again in 2026.

Siwa proved her love for Hughes knows no bounds by teasing her next big step in life was to become a mom.

"That’s my next thing," Siwa teased during a Nov. 2026 appearance on the Petticoat Revolution podcast. "Career is doing her thing. She’s always there. She's been there for 15 years. She'll keep going, she'll keep being there.”

Just days after Siwa expressed her hopes for a baby, her breakup with Hughes was confirmed by multiple outlets, marking an end to their romance 1.5 years after it began.

Editor's Note: The November full supermoon dazzled stargazers with a spectacular show overnight on Nov. 24. Check out our photo wrap article to see spectacular images of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world.

Get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know.

November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter.

Viewers in the U.S. can even get a detailed look at the full moon ahead of local moonrise thanks to a free supermoon livestream from the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP), starting at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) today. The stream will feature live views of the lunar disk captured from the VTP's robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting.

The Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon, because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee, when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant full moon of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon".

November's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon.

Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length.

If you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as the moon will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location.

You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering.

This is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. Check out our full Celestron Nexstar 4SE review for more.

The supermoon will also appear particularly large while close to the horizon, as a phenomenon called the "moon illusion" tricks our brains into thinking that the lunar disk is larger while in the presence of foreground objects compared to when it is overhead.

It'll make for a breathtaking photo opportunity, which you can capitalize on with our beginner's guide to imaging the full moon, along with our picks of the best cameras and lenses for capturing the night sky.

#704. Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

Never before have young people around the world been so well-educated while facing so many economic challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off than my parents?

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests."

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!"

This article was originally published in German.

#703. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising new direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," says Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether."

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures."

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

Materials provided by Utrecht University, Faculty of Science. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
